title: IL-19 promotes psoriasis progression by inhibiting keratinocyte apoptosis via the Bcl-2/Caspase-3 axis.
abstract: BackgroundKeratinocyte apoptosis dysregulation is central to psoriasis pathogenesis. Interleukin-19 (IL-19) is upregulated in psoriatic lesions, but its functional role in apoptotic signaling remains unclear. This study investigated the impact of IL-19 on keratinocyte apoptosis and its underlying mechanism via the Bcl-2/Caspase-3 axis.MethodsClinical samples from psoriasis vulgaris patients (n = 34) and healthy controls (n = 32) were analyzed by immunohistochemistry. In vitro experiments employed M5-stimulated HaCaT cells with IL-19 knockdown/overexpression, assessed by CCK-8, flow cytometry, TUNEL, qPCR and Western blot. In vivo, an imiquimod (IMQ)-induced psoriasis-like mouse model was used to evaluate skin inflammation, apoptosis, and pathway modulation.ResultsIL-19 expression was significantly higher in psoriatic epidermis and correlated positively with Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI) scores. In vitro, IL-19 knockdown promoted keratinocyte apoptosis, reduced Bcl-2, and increased cleaved-caspase-3/PARP; these effects were reversed by IL-19 overexpression. In vivo, IL-19 knockdown ameliorated IMQ-induced psoriasiform skin lesions and epidermal hyperplasia while enhancing keratinocyte apoptosis and modulating Bcl-2/cleaved-caspase-3. Conversely, IL-19 overexpression exacerbated the psoriasiform phenotype and suppressed apoptosis.ConclusionIL-19 promotes epidermal hyperplasia and inhibits keratinocyte apoptosis by regulating the Bcl-2/Caspase-3 signaling axis. These findings not only clarify a key molecular mechanism in psoriasis pathogenesis but also highlight IL-19 and its downstream pathway as promising candidates for targeted therapy.

title: INDIVIDUAL ARTICLE: Clinical and Real-World Implications of IL-17 Receptor Blockade in Plaque Psoriasis and Psoriatic Arthritis With Brodalumab.
abstract: Brodalumab is a fully human monoclonal antibody targeting interleukin-17 receptor A (IL-17RA), providing a mechanistically distinct approach to inhibiting IL-17–mediated inflammation in plaque psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis (approved in Japan). Across pivotal randomized trials and extensive real-world studies, brodalumab demonstrates a rapid onset of action, high rates of complete skin clearance, durable efficacy, and consistent effectiveness across diverse patient subgroups, while randomized and real-world data also support meaningful improvements in joint outcomes among patients with concomitant psoriatic arthritis. This review synthesizes clinical trial and real-world evidence to contextualize the efficacy, safety, and clinical positioning of IL-17RA blockade with brodalumab across the spectrum of psoriatic disease.

title: Cold Stress Activates ACSL1+ Macrophages in a Fatty Acid-Dependent Manner to Exacerbate Psoriasis.
abstract: The relapse of psoriasis precludes a complete cure and can result in multisystem comorbidities, making relapse prevention a critical clinical challenge. Clinically, psoriasis tends to worsen or relapse in winter, but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. In this study, we utilized an imiquimod (IMQ)-induced psoriasis-like mouse model to investigate the role of cold stress in the exacerbation of psoriasis during winter. Our data indicate that cold stress significantly aggravates IMQ-induced psoriatic lesions. While cold stress alone does not directly induce psoriasis, it can promote the development of psoriasis-like lesions in mice exposed to low doses of IMQ. Single-nucleus transcriptome analysis demonstrated that cold stress leads to the remodelling of macrophage phenotypes in psoriatic lesions, with a notable increase in ACSL1+ macrophages. These cells exhibit higher intracellular neutral lipid content and produce more IL-1β, which in turn stimulates γδT cells to secrete more IL-17A. The increase of ACSL1+ macrophages is associated with cold stress-induced lipid synthesis in dermal adipocytes. Notably, the number of ACSL1+ IL-1β + macrophages is significantly increased in the skin of psoriasis patients in winter. Therefore, targeting the formation of ACSL1+ macrophages may be a potential strategy to prevent the worsening of psoriasis in winter.

title: Pathogenesis and clinical features of psoriasis.
abstract: Psoriasis, a papulosquamous skin disease, was originally thought of as a disorder primarily of epidermal keratinocytes, but is now recognised as one of the commonest immune-mediated disorders. Tumour necrosis factor alpha, dendritic cells, and T-cells all contribute substantially to its pathogenesis. In early-onset psoriasis (beginning before age 40 years), carriage of HLA-Cw6 and environmental triggers, such as beta-haemolytic streptococcal infections, are major determinants of disease expression. Moreover, at least nine chromosomal psoriasis susceptibility loci have been identified. Several clinical phenotypes of psoriasis are recognised, with chronic plaque (psoriasis vulgaris) accounting for 90% of cases. Comorbidities of psoriasis are attracting interest, and include impairment of quality of life and associated depressive illness, cardiovascular disease, and a seronegative arthritis known as psoriatic arthritis. A more complete understanding of underlying pathomechanisms is leading to new treatments, which will be discussed in the second part of this Series.

title: A single-cell atlas of IL-23 inhibition in cutaneous psoriasis distinguishes clinical response.
abstract: Psoriasis vulgaris and other chronic inflammatory diseases improve markedly with therapeutic blockade of interleukin-23 (IL-23) signaling, but the genetic mechanisms underlying clinical responses remain poorly understood. Using single-cell transcriptomics, we profiled immune cells isolated from lesional psoriatic skin before and during IL-23 blockade. In clinically responsive patients, a psoriatic transcriptional signature in skin-resident memory T cells was strongly attenuated. In contrast, poorly responsive patients were distinguished by persistent activation of IL-17-producing T (T17) cells, a mechanism distinct from alternative cytokine signaling or resistance isolated to epidermal keratinocytes. Even in IL-23 blockade-responsive patients, we detected a recurring set of recalcitrant, disease-specific transcriptional abnormalities. This irreversible immunological state may necessitate ongoing IL-23 inhibition. Spatial transcriptomic analyses also suggested that successful IL-23 blockade requires dampening of >90% of IL-17-induced response in lymphocyte-adjacent keratinocytes, an unexpectedly high threshold. Collectively, our data establish a patient-level paradigm for dissecting responses to immunomodulatory treatments.

title: Exploring Rare and Atypical Forms of Psoriasis: A Narrative Review.
abstract: Psoriasis is a chronic immune-mediated inflammatory dermatosis characterized by marked clinical heterogeneity. Although plaque psoriasis represents the most common phenotype, several uncommon and atypical variants may pose considerable diagnostic challenges because of their unusual morphology, distribution, and clinicopathological presentation. Early recognition of these rare forms is essential to avoid misdiagnosis and inappropriate management. This narrative review summarizes the current evidence regarding selected atypical variants of psoriasis, including psoriasis gyrata, linear psoriasis, follicular psoriasis, psoriatic onycho-pachydermo-periostitis, psoriatic neurodermatitis, interdigital psoriasis, parakeratosis pustulosa, psoriasis of the lips, psoriasiform acral dermatitis, psoriasis dermatitis, and extreme hyperkeratotic forms. For each entity, we discuss epidemiology, clinical presentation, dermoscopic and histopathological findings, differential diagnosis, pathophysiological hypotheses, and therapeutic considerations. Particular attention is given to distinguishing these entities from inflammatory, infectious, and neoplastic mimickers. The integration of clinical evaluation with dermoscopy and histopathological examination remains crucial in challenging cases. Awareness of these uncommon variants may improve diagnostic accuracy and facilitate timely therapeutic intervention.

sections.results:
Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease affecting approximately 2–3% of the global population and is currently recognized as a complex immune-mediated disorder involving genetic susceptibility, environmental triggers, and dysregulated innate and adaptive immune responses []. While chronic plaque psoriasis is the most prevalent phenotype, psoriasis encompasses a broad clinical spectrum including guttate, erythrodermic, inverse, pustular, and palmoplantar variants. The considerable heterogeneity in morphology, anatomical distribution, clinical course, and therapeutic response among these phenotypes supports the concept of psoriasis as a spectrum of related diseases rather than a single nosological entity []. In most cases, the diagnosis of psoriasis is established clinically; however, rare and atypical forms may closely mimic infectious, inflammatory, or neoplastic dermatoses. Histology can become crucial in the diagnosis of these more complex forms of psoriasis, which can present a clinical challenge even to trained dermatologists.

This narrative review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of rare and atypical variants of psoriasis, focusing on their clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, dermoscopic and histopathological characteristics, pathogenic mechanisms, and available therapeutic strategies.

A narrative review of the literature was performed using PubMed/MEDLINE and Scopus databases, with no time restrictions. Articles published in English and relevant historical reports were screened using combinations of the following keywords: “rare psoriasis”, “atypical psoriasis”, “linear psoriasis”, “follicular psoriasis”, “psoriasis gyrata”, “psoriatic neurodermatitis”, “interdigital psoriasis”, “parakeratosis pustulosa”, and “psoriatic onycho-pachydermo-periostitis”. Case reports, case series, observational studies, and review articles were considered. Additional references were identified from the bibliographies of selected articles. After removing duplicates, 39 articles were included in the final synthesis. This review was not conducted as a systematic review.

Bibliometrics was used to conduct frequency analysis. This quantitative analysis serves to stratify the variants, distinguishing between those that are relatively common in clinical reporting and those that remain exceptionally rare.

We identified 11 clinical presentations corresponding to rare and atypical variants of psoriasis ():

Psoriasis Gyrata (PG) Linear Psoriasis (LP) Follicular Psoriasis (FP) Psoriatic Onycho-Pachydermo-Periostitis (POPP) Psoriatic Neurodermatitis (PN) Interdigital Psoriasis (IP) Parakeratosis Pustulosa (PP) Psoriasis of the lips Psoriasiform acral dermatitis (PAD) Psoriasis Dermatitis (PD) Extreme hyperkeratotic forms

LP, FP, and PP emerged with the highest publication volumes. PG and PN, together with the extreme hyperkeratotic forms, demonstrated the lowest literature volumes.

PG is a very particular form distinguished by the singular form and distribution of the scaly patches that constitute large arabesque-like lesions. These are tortuous and vermiform, or circular and semicircular with tortuous appendages, mainly affecting the trunk (). These can be interpreted as the result of annular lesions evolving into polycyclic patterns [].

The molecular mechanisms driving the concentric, gyrate expansion of lesions remain partially elusive. However, comparative studies on migratory patterns of T-cells and keratinocytes suggest a “reaction-diffusion” wave phenomenon. In PG, the local concentration of specific chemokines (such as CXCL8 and CXCL10) drives a rapid, centrifugal migration of neutrophils and Th17/Th1 cells. This outpaces the central resolution capacity of regulatory T-cells, leaving a cleared or less inflamed center and a highly active, advancing gyrate border [].

The main differential diagnoses of PG include conditions with annular or polycyclic lesions such as tinea corporis, lichen planus annulare, nummular eczema, erythema annulare centrifugum, secondary syphilis, erythema marginatum, erythema gyratum repens (EGR), and erythema multiforme annulare. EGR is the most critical pitfall; unlike EGR, PG scales are typically micaceous and silvery, histological features remain strictly psoriatic, and its progression rate is significantly slower.

First-line therapies combine topical corticosteroids with vitamin D analogs and phototherapy; moderate-to-severe cases require systemic treatments, including biologics.

LP is an exceptionally rare clinical variant of psoriasis, characterized by psoriatic plaques distributed along Blaschko’s lines, typically in a linear pattern (). The condition exhibits two distinct profiles: isolated LP, not associated with classical psoriasis, and superimposed LP, occurring concomitantly with classical psoriasis []. Pustular LP, a rarer subtype, has also been observed []. The pathogenesis of LP remains unclear but is thought to involve genetic mosaicism. Happle’s theory suggests that linear manifestations result from a postzygotic mutation during embryogenesis, leading to loss of heterozygosity at a predisposing gene locus []. Genomic sequencing studies on microdissected linear tissue have confirmed this hypothesis. In patients with superimposed LP, next-generation sequencing has identified postzygotic somatic mutations in genes that regulate the IL-17/IL-23 axis or the NF-kB pathway (such as CARD14 or TRAF3IP2). In isolated LP, the mutation is confined strictly to the Blaschko-linear keratinocytes. In superimposed LP, a second-hit somatic mutation occurs on a background of an inherited, germline heterozygous predisposing mutation, sparking an exacerbated, treatment-resistant localized flare [].

Distinguishing LP from other dermatoses in the Blaschko linear group is challenging. The main differential diagnosis is inflammatory linear verrucous epidermal nevus (ILVEN). Unlike LP, ILVEN typically presents at birth or during infancy, progresses slowly, and exhibits unilateral warty, pruritic lesions arranged in a linear pattern, often on the lower limbs. ILVEN lesions are more resistant to treatment compared to LP, which usually develops later in life, progresses rapidly, and responds to antipsoriatic therapy []. Other conditions, such as Blaschko-linear lichen planus or lichen striatus, can be ruled out with histological examination [].

Local treatments, including topical corticosteroids and other antipsoriatic agents, are less effective in LP compared to classical psoriasis []. Also, biotechnological therapy has shown variable efficacy: linear lesions remain highly resistant, likely due to the altered, autonomous hyper-responsiveness of the mutated mosaic keratinocyte clone [].

FP is a rare and underreported clinical variant of psoriasis, originally described by MacLeod in 1921. It is characterized by hyperkeratotic follicular papules (). This condition has been proposed as a potential initial form of psoriasis that may later progress to other subtypes or remain localized to follicular lesions for an extended period [,]. The pathogenesis of FP is not fully understood: it is thought to represent an early manifestation of psoriasis, with lesions originating around hair follicles.

Two clinical subtypes of FP have been described: the adult variant, predominantly affecting women, with discrete, follicular, hyperkeratotic papules concentrated on the thighs; and the variant affecting the trunk, axillae, and extensor aspects of the extremities, presenting as asymmetric, clustered follicular keratotic papules []. It is also described as flexural and mucosal involvement. Follicular lesions are sometimes seen adjacent to chronic plaque psoriasis, highlighting their potential relationship to more classic psoriatic presentations []. This condition is more frequently reported in children, although many adult cases are described [].

Dermoscopy plays an essential role in identifying psoriatic follicular lesions. Typical dermoscopic findings in FP include a white-brown or pink-white perifollicular background, perifollicular scaling, and vascular features such as dotted vessels, twisted red loops, glomerular vessels, and red globules [,]. Histopathological findings include dilated follicular openings, follicular hyperkeratosis, perifollicular parakeratosis, parakeratotic plugging, hypogranulosis, Munro’s microabscesses, suprapapillary thinning, and tortuous, dilated upper dermal blood vessels [,,]. The differential diagnosis of FP includes pityriasis rubra pilaris, lichen spinulosus, follicular eczema, keratosis pilaris, and follicular lichen planus [].

Therapy begins with topical agents like steroid-salicylic acid combinations; for persistent or widespread cases, therapeutic approaches escalate to phototherapy and systemic drugs, including biologics [].

POPP, first described by Fournier in 1980, is a rare variant of psoriatic disease characterized by the isolated involvement of distal phalanges, particularly of the big toe []. Clinically, it presents with onychodystrophy, including onycholysis and longitudinal striations of the nail plate, painful swelling of the surrounding soft tissues (), and acral bone changes []. Affected nails may exhibit oil spots and pitting [].

In POPP, mechanical stress or micro-trauma triggers an innate immune response at the enthesis. The pathogenesis involves the extension of psoriatic inflammation from the nail bed to the underlying bone through entheses, resulting in periosteal thickening and osteitis similar to other psoriatic enthesopathies [].

Scintigraphy is particularly sensitive in detecting early-stage disease, revealing intense focal uptake in the distal phalanx even when clinical and radiological findings are minimal. Radiological findings include solid periosteal reactions (and “tuft-like” or “brush-like” periosteal reactions) and acral bone thickening, often described as “ivory phalanx”. There is a total absence of involvement of the distal interphalangeal joints, distinguishing POPP from psoriatic arthritis [,]. An association with the HLA-B27 antigen and, more specifically, HLA-B39 has been noted, suggesting a genetic predisposition [].

The differential diagnosis for POPP includes distal interphalangeal psoriatic arthritis, suppurative acrodermatitis continua of Hallopeau, gout, hypertrophic osteoarthropathy, and severe onychomycosis [,]. Therapeutic options for POPP include intralesional steroid injections into the nail matrix and systemic treatments like methotrexate and cyclosporine. In severe and recalcitrant cases, biological drugs (such as adalimumab, etanercept, secukinumab, or ixekizumab) show superior efficacy in halting both soft-tissue swelling and underlying bone remodeling [].

PN typically exhibits erythematous, scaly plaques localized predominantly on the extremities []. Unlike plaque psoriasis, PN plaques are fewer in number and smaller in size (median 4 cm). The hallmark feature of PN plaques is lichenification, which manifests as exaggerated skin lines forming a crisscross pattern (). This lichenified texture is more typical of Lichen Simplex Chronicus (LSC) but is seen in PN without the associated excoriations that are commonly observed in LSC plaques.

A key distinction of PN is its anatomical distribution. Lesions are predominantly confined to the extremities, with bilateral involvement of the knees and elbows being the most frequent pattern. This contrasts with LSC, which often involves the nape of the neck, vulva, feet, and occasionally the anogenital region. Itching is a dominant symptom in both conditions, but patients with PN reported less severe pruritus during rest compared to those with typical LSC.

The pathogenesis of PN remains under debate, highlighting the complex interplay between the peripheral nervous system and immune-mediated cutaneous inflammation (the neuro-cutaneous axis). PN lesions reveal a significant upregulation of nerve growth factor and an increased density of calcitonin gene-related peptide-positive and Substance P-positive unmyelinated C-fibers.

PN may represent a form of LSC superimposed on plaque psoriasis or arise through the Koebner phenomenon in predisposed individuals with psoriasis, since dermoscopy of PN reveals features indicative of both LSC and psoriasis. These include scales, regular linear vessels, and hyperkeratosis. Histologically, PN plaques show several findings typical of psoriasis, including hyperkeratosis, confluent parakeratosis, hypogranulosis, acanthosis, and thinning of suprapapillary layers. PN plaques lacked hallmark features such as spongiform pustules and vertical thick collagen bundles typically observed in LSC.

Psychiatric comorbidities are notable in PN patients, above all depressive disorders and generalized anxiety [].

IP, first named ‘psoriasis alba’ by Waisman, represents a localized intertriginous form of psoriasis (commonly classified as psoriasis inversa). IP typically presents as whitish, sodden, sharply demarcated plaques or patches located between the toes () []. These lesions are firm, pliant, and leathery on palpation, distinguishing them from the soft, macerated appearance of interdigital fungal infection; however, mycological investigations, including direct microscopy and fungal cultures, are essential in ruling out infections []. Pruritus is either absent or mild, and patients often remain asymptomatic. The condition predominantly affects the intertoe spaces of one or both feet; remarkably, interdigital psoriasis is rarely observed between the fingers [].

The unique localization to interdigital spaces may be influenced by friction, moisture, and maceration, potentially triggering the Koebner phenomenon []. Recent studies have revealed a complex bi-directional relationship: frictional trauma induces the psoriatic plaque with an altered, hyperkeratotic skin barrier; the compromised interdigital barrier allows for secondary fungal colonization, triggering an upregulation of IL-23 []. The persistent hydration alters the optical properties of the stratum corneum, causing the classic “whitish” and sodden appearance, which masks the underlying erythema typical of classic plaque psoriasis.

Histological examination of IP reveals features consistent with psoriasis, although with some variations. Common findings include confluent hyperparakeratosis, intermittent stratum granulosum, and psoriasiform hyperplasia. Occasionally, subcorneal micropustules (e.g., Kogoj pustules) may be observed, while Munro microabscesses are typically absent. Periodic acid-Schiff staining is negative, aiding in the exclusion of fungal infections [].

The management of IP is similar to other forms of intertriginous psoriasis. Topical therapies, including corticosteroids and vitamin D analogs, are effective in most cases [].

PP is a unique pediatric nail condition. The disease commonly affects a single finger, typically the thumb or index finger, and is characterized by mild eczematous changes in the fingertip pulp combined with psoriasiform alterations of the nail (). The condition usually begins with pustules or vesicles on the pulp, progressing to mild eczematous changes, and occasionally leading to pulpitis. Nail changes, which typically follow the skin inflammatory phase, include mild subungual hyperkeratosis and onycholysis, often more pronounced on one side of the nail. Spontaneous remission is frequent []. Acrodermatitis continua of Hallopeau remains the most common misdiagnosis in these patients: it is more common in adults, though it can also be observed in childhood; it usually has a more aggressive course with the presence of pustular lesions, pain, potential nail deformity, and osteolysis; it rarely resolves spontaneously. The differential diagnosis for PP also includes onychomycosis, distinguished by fungal culture and microscopy; chronic paronychia, identified by persistent inflammation of the proximal nail fold, nail sucking, typically observed in younger children with evident behavioral habits, and eczema, which may overlap with PP, but patch testing can help rule out allergic contact dermatitis [].

The progression of PP to nail psoriasis has been documented in some patients, suggesting a potential overlap between PP and early psoriatic nail disease [].

Psoriasis of the lips typically presents with scaling, fissuring, and erythema, often accompanied by discomfort such as a burning sensation and difficulty during eating or speaking. Lesions may involve one or both lips, with extension over the vermilion border (), while the remaining oral mucosa generally appears unaffected. In some cases, lip involvement may occur in association with other psoriatic lesions [].

Dermoscopy of the lip lesions demonstrates diffuse, monomorphic dots and globular vessels, accompanied by white scales []. Psoriasis of the lips, however, can be clinically misdiagnosed as chronic eczema, actinic cheilitis, chronic candidiasis, or leukoplakia. The white color of psoriatic scales in dermoscopy, in contrast to the yellow scales of dermatitis, is a particularly valuable diagnostic clue [].

Since 2000, only fifteen cases of psoriasis affecting the lips have been identified through our screening methodology. Psoriasis of the lips can precede or follow the appearance of classic psoriatic lesions.

The term PAD was coined by Zaias in 1980 [,,]. PAD is a rare and distinctive form of dermatitis that primarily affects the distal phalanges of the fingers, with a notable shortening of the nail bed. The lesions are typically psoriasiform in nature, characterized by erythema, scaling, and fissures on the palmar surfaces of the digits, often accompanied by a sclerodermoid appearance of the dorsal aspects of the fingers [].

While PAD may present isolated, it can also occur in conjunction with typical psoriatic lesions in other areas of the body. It has been primarily observed in children. The differential diagnosis of PAD includes other acral dermatitis conditions such as contact dermatitis, dyshidrotic eczema, and atopic dermatitis. However, the absence of a personal or family history of atopy, negative patch tests, and normal serum IgE levels in the observed cases point against these diagnoses [].

Histologically, PAD presents as a subacute dermatitis with a dense lymphocytic infiltrate, massive spongiosis, parakeratosis, scale crusts, psoriasiform acanthosis, and exocytosis; this has led some to consider PAD a separate entity, distinct from psoriasis []. However, the concurrent presence of classic psoriatic lesions elsewhere in the body, along with nail dystrophy, suggests that PAD may in fact be a particular variant of acral psoriasis in children [].

The pathogenesis of PAD is not fully understood; it may be genetically predisposed, as it frequently occurs in children who later develop typical psoriasis lesions in other areas of the body. Environmental factors, such as seasonal changes, seem to influence the severity of PAD, with some patients showing improvement during summer holidays at the seaside []. The pathogenesis of nail shortening observed in PAD is believed to be related to hypertrophy of the cuticle, secondary to the inflammation, rather than a permanent anatomical change in the nail bed [].

While it is often resistant to treatment and can cause significant disability when multiple fingers are involved, it may resolve spontaneously during puberty [].

PD is a condition characterized by a blend of clinical features of both psoriasis and atopic dermatitis (AD). The condition is particularly observed in children, and its understanding is evolving as researchers explore the overlap between these two diseases. It has been proposed as a spectrum of disease rather than a distinct pathology, possibly due to shared immune activation mechanisms between AD and psoriasis. PD represents an intermediate phenotype between these two disorders, manifesting features from both [,,,].

Children with PD often present with facial lesions, a feature more commonly associated with AD, while the scalp is less frequently affected compared to children with psoriasis. Lesions may also occur on the body, resembling psoriasis, but without the classic well-demarcated plaques. The presence of eczema-like changes in the acute phase of PD, along with psoriasiform changes later, is a key feature distinguishing it from both pure AD and psoriasis []. Additionally, lesions can be found on areas that typically present with psoriasis, such as elbows, knees, and the torso [,].

Although psoriasis involves type 17 immune responses, atopic dermatitis is centered on type 2 and type 22 responses, with common type 1 polarization in chronic lesions. Recently, it has been observed that some cytokines involved in the pathogenic mechanisms of psoriasis (IL-17, IL-17C, and IL-23) are also implicated in the chronic phase of atopic dermatitis, as evidenced by the effectiveness of some psoriasis-targeted drugs, such as ustekinumab, in the treatment of moderate to severe chronic AD [,]. While Th17 cells drive inflammation in psoriasis and Th2 cells are central to AD, evidence suggests a concurrent activation of Th17 and Th2 pathways in PD. This mixed immune response could explain the overlapping features, where skin barrier dysfunction typical of AD is coupled with inflammatory processes seen in psoriasis [,,,].

Unlike psoriasis, nail involvement appears to be absent in PD. Conversely, involvement of the feet, glutes, and genitalia is more common than in AD, while facial and neck lesions are less frequent []. Histological findings in PD are limited but suggest that PD shares features of both psoriasis and AD. Skin biopsies often demonstrate psoriasiform hyperplasia, hypogranulosis, spongiosis, and eosinophilic infiltrates []. Moreover, studies suggest that metabolic comorbidities, such as obesity, are more common in PD patients compared to those with either psoriasis or AD alone.

The diagnosis of PD remains challenging due to its mixed features and lack of universal criteria, often relying on clinical features. In the differential diagnosis of psoriasiform dermatitis (PD), the findings most suggestive of psoriasis include erythro-squamous plaques on the body and/or extremities, pustules excluding facial pustules, and erythema of the anal cleft. Conversely, features more supportive of atopic dermatitis include eczema and/or lichenification of the flexural areas, dyshidrotic eczema, and Dennie–Morgan folds and/or periorbital darkening. reports the complete ranking of clinical features suggestive of psoriasis and atopic dermatitis, according to Müller et al. [,].

With regard to treatment, although randomized controlled trials are still needed to define the optimal therapeutic approach for PD, a practical decision-making algorithm has recently been proposed. This algorithm takes into account different clinical scenarios according to whether PD is primary or induced by biologic therapies targeting the Th1/Th17 or Th2 pathways [].

Extreme hyperkeratotic variants of psoriasis are characterized by a marked accumulation of thick, adherent scales and are often relatively resistant to conventional topical therapies. In the literature, the terms used to describe these forms are sometimes applied interchangeably; however, several clinical features may help distinguish rupioid, ostraceous, and elephantine psoriasis.

Rupioid psoriasis derives its name from the Greek word rhupos , meaning filth or dirt, and was first described in 1948. Clinically, it is characterized by dark, extremely thick, well-demarcated hyperkeratotic plaques arranged in concentric layers. These lesions often assume a conical morphology, resembling a limpet shell. The “dirty” appearance reflects the presence of thick crusts, serosanguineous exudate, and marked epidermal hyperplasia. Recent observations suggest that psoriasis with very thick plaques may show a male predominance and may be associated with a higher frequency of psoriatic arthritis and nail involvement, as well as a greater affected body surface area compared with thin-plaque psoriasis [,].

Ostraceous psoriasis shares several features with rupioid psoriasis but typically presents with oval, circular, or ring-like hyperkeratotic plaques with a concave surface, closely resembling an oyster shell. The scales are usually thick, firmly adherent, and difficult to remove. This variant is also considered poorly responsive to topical treatment and has been reported in association with psoriatic arthritis [].

Elephantine psoriasis represents another severe hyperkeratotic phenotype, presenting with exceptionally thick, extensive, silvery-white scaly plaques that may cover large areas of the body and resemble elephant skin (). Lesions are most frequently described on the back, buttocks, upper limbs, and lower limbs. Histopathological findings may include marked papillomatosis and alternating areas of hypogranulosis and hypergranulosis [].

A key differential diagnosis of hyperkeratotic psoriasis is ILVEN; although ILVEN typically follows the lines of Blaschko, it shares many histological features with psoriasis, specifically the presence of alternating bands of hypergranulosis and hypogranulosis. For lesions displaying a rupioid morphology, clinicians must also consider secondary or late latent rupioid syphilis, keratotic scabies, reactive arthritis, and disseminated histoplasmosis []. Other reported differential diagnoses for these hyperkeratotic forms include verrucous Darier’s disease, acquired palmoplantar keratoderma, and photosensitive skin lesions associated with aminoaciduria.

Rare and atypical variants of psoriasis remain diagnostically challenging because of their unusual morphology, atypical localization, and overlap with numerous inflammatory and infectious dermatoses. Although an experienced dermatologist should be able to recognize most presentations, some variants may require additional investigations to avoid diagnostic pitfalls. Dermoscopy, reflectance confocal microscopy, and optical coherence tomography can provide valuable diagnostic support; nevertheless, histopathological examination remains the gold standard when clinical findings are inconclusive.

Accurate recognition of these uncommon forms is clinically important, as misdiagnosis may lead to unnecessary investigations and inappropriate treatments, particularly repeated courses of antifungals or antibiotics. Moreover, certain variants, such as psoriatic onycho-pachydermo-periostitis, may signal underlying musculoskeletal involvement requiring multidisciplinary management.

The pathogenesis of these rare presentations remains incompletely understood and may involve mechanisms such as genetic mosaicism, Koebnerisation, follicular-centered inflammation, or localized enthesopathy. Whether they represent distinct pathogenetic entities or simply phenotypic expressions within the psoriatic spectrum remains to be clarified.

Dermatology is a profoundly visual specialty, confirming the well-known axiom that “you diagnose what you already know” []. The peculiar clinical features reviewed here support this concept: once recognized, these variants become considerably easier to identify. However, current therapeutic evidence remains limited, being derived largely from case reports and small case series, highlighting the need for multicenter studies to establish evidence-based diagnostic and treatment strategies.

sections.abstract:
To investigate the role and molecular mechanisms of the deacetylase SIRT6 in psoriasis and evaluate its potential as a therapeutic target for topical treatment.

The expression of SIRT6 in psoriatic lesions and healthy skin was analyzed using datasets from the GEO database. In vitro, Human Immortalized Epidermal Cells (HaCaT) were stimulated with TNF-α to establish a psoriasis-like cellular model. SIRT6 was overexpressed or knocked down in HaCaT cells to evaluate its effects on keratinocyte inflammation, proliferation, and migration. Integrated transcriptomic analysis and subsequent validation were conducted to explore the signaling pathways regulated by SIRT6. Changes in mRNA expression, protein levels and inflammatory cytokine secretion were assessed by RT–qPCR, Western blotting, immunohistochemistry, and ELISA. Therapeutic potential was assessed using a SIRT6 inhibitor-loaded alginate/carbomer hydrogel in an imiquimod-induced psoriasiform dermatitis mouse model and in human psoriatic skin explants ex vivo.

GEO dataset analysis revealed that SIRT6 expression was significantly higher in psoriatic lesions than in either healthy controls or non-lesional skin (both p < 0.0001) and significantly decreased after treatment with biologic agents or JAK inhibitors ( p < 0.05 vs pre-treatment). In HaCaT cells, TNF‑α stimulation upregulated SIRT6 by 1.5-fold ( p <0.01). Overexpression of SIRT6 enhanced TNF-α-induced production of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-23, and TNF-α) and the alarmins S100A8 and S100A9, while promoting keratinocyte proliferation and migration, whereas SIRT6 knockdown produced opposite effects. Combined transcriptomic profiling and multiple validation assays (qPCR, Western blot, and immunohistochemistry) revealed that SIRT6 overexpression activated the STAT signaling pathway by downregulating SOCS2 and upregulating STAT1/3 phosphorylation, while SIRT6 knockdown or inhibition yielded the opposite outcomes. Topical administration of the SIRT6 inhibitor-loaded hydrogel alleviated imiquimod-induced psoriasiform dermatitis in mice and reduced inflammatory responses in human psoriatic skin explants.

SIRT6 exacerbates psoriasiform inflammation by modulating the SOCS2–STAT1/3 signaling pathway. These findings suggest that topical inhibition of SIRT6 may represent a potential therapeutic strategy for psoriasis.
sections.other:
Psoriasis is a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory skin disease characterized by erythema and scaling, with a global prevalence of approximately 2–3%. The IL-23/IL-17 axis plays a central role in psoriasis, and the remarkable clinical efficacy of monoclonal antibodies targeting IL-17, and IL-23 underscores the core function of these cytokines as key drivers of the disease. Although biologics have achieved groundbreaking significance in the treatment of psoriasis, their high cost imposes a substantial financial burden on patients. Moreover, challenges persist in managing refractory or recurrent skin lesions. Therefore, topical agents such as corticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors, and vitamin D3 analogues remain a cost-effective treatment option. However, long-term use of corticosteroids may lead to adverse reactions such as local skin atrophy, telangiectasia, and pigmentation abnormalities. Therefore, it remains important to continue investigating the pathogenesis of psoriasis and to identify novel therapeutic targets for its treatment.

Sirtuin 6 (SIRT6) is a member of the NAD + - dependent class III histone deacetylase family and plays critical roles in cellular proliferation, genomic stability, and inflammatory regulation. Elevated SIRT6 expression has been reported in skin tumors such as metastatic melanoma and squamous cell carcinoma, where it promotes tumor cell proliferation. Mechanistically, SIRT6 is predominantly localized in the nucleus, where it deacetylates histones H3K9 and H3K56, thereby regulating chromatin structure, gene transcription, and DNA damage repair. In addition to its nuclear functions, SIRT6 can localize to the cytoplasm and endoplasmic reticulum under stress conditions and has been shown to regulate TNF-α secretion through deacylation of its precursor protein at K19 and K20., Emerging evidence suggests a potential involvement of SIRT6 in psoriasis. Increased SIRT6 expression has been observed in psoriatic lesions, imiquimod-induced mouse models, and psoriasis-related cell models., In addition, functional studies have suggested that SIRT6 may contribute to keratinocyte hyperproliferation and inflammatory responses in psoriasis. However, whether SIRT6 acts as a direct amplifier of inflammatory signaling pathways in psoriasis has not been systematically investigated. Therefore, in the present study, we aimed to investigate the pathogenic role of SIRT6 in psoriasis, with a particular focus on its involvement in inflammatory signaling mechanisms, and to evaluate the therapeutic potential of a topically applied SIRT6 inhibitor-loaded hydrogel.
sections.methods:
All datasets were downloaded from NCBI ( https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/gds/ ). After combining GSE13355 and GSE14905 , the SVA package was used to remove batch effects. The data were then divided into SIRT6 high-expression and low-expression groups based on the median value of SIRT6 expression, and gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) was performed using the ClusterProfiler package. The datasets ( GSE13355 , GSE14905 , GSE117239 , GSE178228 , and GSE69967 ) are publicly available from the GEO database and have been de-identified. According to the policy of Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hospital, Sun Yat-sen University, this secondary analysis of publicly available data was exempt from ethical approval.

HaCaT cells were purchased from Cobioer Biosciences Co., Ltd. (Nanjing, China) and sent to Immocell Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Xiamen, China) for STR profiling. The cells were cultured in complete medium consisting of 90% DMEM (Gibco, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) and 10% FBS (Gibco) at 37°C in a 5% CO 2 atmosphere. Recombinant Human TNF-α, Oncostatin M (OSM), IL-1α, IL-22, and IL-17A were purchased from PeproTech, Inc. (New Jersey, USA). HaCaT cells were stimulated with either TNF-α, IL-17A, IL-1α alone, or a mixture of five pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, OSM, IL-1α, IL-22, and IL-17A), known as M5, to establish a psoriasis-like cell model.

The SIRT6 overexpressing lentivirus (Cat. No. CL097) and the negative control lentivirus (Cat. No. LV587) were purchased from Applied Biological Materials Inc. (Shanghai, China). The overexpression lentivirus carries the full-length wild-type coding sequence (CDS) of the human SIRT6 gene based on the reference sequence NM_016539.4 (NCBI Gene ID: 51548). Transfection was performed according to the manufacturer’s instructions with a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 100, and Polybrene was added at 5 μg/mL during the transfection to enhance transfection efficiency.

After stimulation with TNF-α, total RNA was extracted from control-transfected and SIRT6-overexpressing HaCaT cells (three biological replicates per group) using RNAiso Plus (Takara, Japan). The RNA samples were subsequently sent to Novogene Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China) for cDNA library construction and sequencing on the Illumina platform. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were identified by meeting both screening criteria: |log2 fold change (log2FC)| ≥ 0.585 and adjusted P-value (Padj) < 0.05. The use of the commercial HaCaT cell line in this study was exempt from ethical approval according to the policy of Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hospital, Sun Yat-sen University.

Small interfering RNA was used to knock down SIRT6 in HaCaT cells, and three siRNA targeting human SIRT6 were synthesized by Geneyuan Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Guangzhou, China). The si-SIRT6-1 sequences were: sense strand, 5’-CCAAGUGUAAGACGCAGUATT-3’; antisense strand, 5’-UACUGCGUCUUACACUUGGTT-3’. The si-SIRT6-2 sequences were: sense strand,5’-GGCUACGUUGACGAGGUCATT-3’; antisense strand, 5’-UGACCUCGUCAACGUAGCCTT-3’. The si-SIRT6-3 sequences were: sense strand, 5’-CAAGUUCGACACCACCUUUTT-3’; antisense strand, 5’-AAAGGUGGUGUCGAACUUGTT-3’. The si-SIRT6-1 exhibited the best knockdown efficiency and stability and was used in subsequent experiments. Transfection was performed when the cell density reached 30%-50%, and Lipofectamine 3000 reagent (Thermo Fisher, USA) was used to enhance transfection efficiency.

Total RNA extraction, reverse transcription into cDNA, and RT-qPCR reactions were performed using the corresponding kits (EZBioscience, Suzhou, China) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Quantitative PCR was conducted using the LightCycler ® 480 System (Roche, Switzerland).

Total protein was extracted using RIPA lysis buffer. Equal amounts of protein were separated by SDS-PAGE and transferred onto PVDF membranes. After blocking, the membranes were incubated with primary antibodies overnight at 4 °C, followed by incubation with the corresponding secondary antibodies at room temperature for 1 h. All primary antibodies were purchased from Cell Signaling Technology (MA, USA) or Abcam (Cambridge, UK). Protein bands were detected using an enhanced chemiluminescence system. β-tubulin was used as the internal control.

Cell culture supernatants from HaCaT cells under different treatment conditions were collected. The concentrations of IL-6 and IL-23 were determined using commercially available ELISA kits (Elabscience, Wuhan, China) according to the manufacturers’ instructions.

Human and mouse skin specimens were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde and embedded in paraffin. Sections (4 μm) were deparaffinized, rehydrated, and heat-treated for antigen retrieval. After blocking, sections were incubated overnight at 4°C with primary antibodies against target proteins, including anti-SIRT6 (1:500), anti-SOCS2 (1:200), anti-p-STAT1 (1:200), and anti-p-STAT3 (1:200). Sections were sequentially incubated with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies, developed with DAB, and counterstained with hematoxylin for microscopic observation. Semi-quantitative analysis of immunostaining intensity was performed using ImageJ software in at least five random high-power fields (×200) per section.

All wild-type (WT) and SIRT6-transgenic (SIRT6-Tg; official strain name: C57BL/6-Tg (RP23-352G18)1Coppa/J) mice used in this study were female C57BL/6 mice aged 6–8 weeks. Mice were purchased from the Laboratory Animal Center of Sun Yat-sen University (Guangzhou, China) and housed under specific pathogen-free conditions. Psoriasiform skin inflammation was induced in mice by topical application of 5% imiquimod (IMQ; 3M Pharmaceuticals, St. Paul, MN, USA). Briefly, 62.5 mg of IMQ cream was applied daily to the shaved dorsal skin or 20 mg to the ears for six consecutive days. Randomization was used to allocate mice to different experimental groups. Each group contained 5–8 mice, and all experiments were independently repeated twice. The ear thickness of mice was measured using a micrometer to assess the overall severity of skin inflammation. The severity of psoriasiform dermatitis was assessed using the psoriasis severity index (PSI), which evaluates erythema, scaling, and skin thickening. Additional outcome measures included dorsal epidermal thickness, histopathological changes and immunohistochemical staining of skin tissues, and alterations in skin mRNA expression levels. Total RNA was extracted using a tissue RNA Purification Kit (EZBioscience, Suzhou, China). The researchers responsible for IMQ administration and treatment were aware of the group allocation but were not involved in the subsequent assessment or data analysis, while those conducting the outcome measurements and analyses were kept blinded to the group assignments. Mice were anesthetized with 1% sodium pentobarbital (50 mg/kg, intraperitoneal injection). After confirming deep anesthesia, the animals were euthanized by cervical dislocation. All experimental procedures were performed in accordance with ethical guidelines for animal protection and were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee at Sun Yat-sen University (Approval No. SYSU-IACUC-2025-000931).

A hydrogel matrix containing 4% alginate, 1% Carbomer 940, and 5% glycerol was prepared as previously described. And the prepared hydrogel was stored at 4°C. To prepare the SIRT6 inhibitor hydrogel, the OSS_128167 (MCE, Shanghai, China) was added to the hydrogel at a concentration of 1 mg per mL and thoroughly mixed via ultrasonication.

Psoriatic lesions were obtained from three patients with newly diagnosed psoriasis using a punch biopsy, and the patients had not received any topical or systemic medication for at least one month prior. Informed consent for the collection and subsequent use of the lesions was obtained from the patients. This study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Medical Ethics Committee of Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hospital, Sun Yat-sen University (Approval No. SYSKY-2025-1014-01). Each lesion was evenly divided into two equal pieces (approximately 0.5 cm × 0.5 cm × 0.5 cm). Vehicle hydrogel or SIRT6 inhibitor-loaded hydrogel was topically applied to the surface of each piece, respectively. The explants were cultured in complete medium at the air–liquid interface with the epidermal side facing upward. After 24 hours of culture, RNA was extracted from the tissues for RT-qPCR analysis.

All data are presented as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). Statistical comparisons between two groups were performed using two-tailed Student’s t-tests. For comparisons involving three or more groups, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was applied, followed by appropriate post-hoc tests (Tukey’s or Dunnett’s) as indicated. The specific statistical tests used for each experiment are clearly stated in the corresponding figure legends. All statistical analyses and graphing were performed using R (version 4.5.1) or GraphPad Prism (version 8.0.2). A P-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
sections.results:
First, to determine the expression of SIRT6 in skin tissues, we compared the gene expression levels of SIRT6 in lesional and non-lesional tissues from psoriasis patients and in healthy skin tissues from the GEO database. In the GSE13355 and GSE14905 microarray datasets, SIRT6 gene expression levels were significantly higher in psoriatic lesions than in non-lesional and healthy skin (). Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) of the two datasets indicated that high SIRT6 expression was associated with the upregulation of E2F transcription factors, the G2M cell cycle, the IL6_JAK_STAT3 signaling pathway, and the inflammatory response pathway (). Additionally, analysis of the GSE117239 , GSE178228 , and GSE69967 datasets revealed that SIRT6 gene expression in psoriatic lesions was downregulated after separate treatment with anti-IL-12/23, anti-TNF-α, and anti-IL-17A monoclonal antibodies, as well as Janus kinase inhibitors (). SIRT6 protein is primarily localized in the nucleus, with minor presence in the cytoplasm and endoplasmic reticulum. We assessed SIRT6 protein expression in skin tissues via immunohistochemical staining. Psoriatic keratinocytes exhibited significantly higher nuclear SIRT6 expression levels and positivity rates of nuclear staining than healthy controls ( and ). The above results indicated that both the gene and protein expression levels of SIRT6 were elevated in psoriatic lesions, and this increase in SIRT6 might be associated with signaling pathways related to proliferation and inflammation.

5% Imiquimod (IMQ) application is a well-established method for inducing PsD in mice. After six consecutive days of topical treatment with Vaseline (as control) or IMQ on the dorsal skin of wild-type (WT) and SIRT6 transgenic (SIRT6-Tg) mice, the SIRT6-Tg mice displayed exacerbated PsD compared to WT mice on day 6 (). The PSI score, which assesses the severity of erythema, scaling, and induration, was used to evaluate the severity of skin lesion. SIRT6-Tg mice exhibited significantly higher PSI scores than WT mice on day 6 (). IMQ induced epidermal thickening in mice, and the thickening was more pronounced in SIRT6-Tg mice than in WT mice after IMQ treatment ( and ). IMQ-treated mice developed psoriasis-like pathological changes, including epidermal alterations and dermal inflammatory cells infiltration. The Baker scores, used to evaluate these pathological changes, were higher in SIRT6-Tg mice than in WT mice (). This finding suggested that SIRT6, by aggravating IMQ-induced PsD in mice, could play a role in psoriasis development.

We established a psoriasis cell model by TNF-α-stimulated human immortalized epidermal cell (HaCaT cell). In this cell model, treatment with TNF-α at concentrations of 40 ng/mL or higher significantly increased SIRT6 expression compared to unstimulated controls, and this increase was observed in a concentration-dependent manner ( and ). However, under other stimulation conditions, such as IL-17A (200 ng/mL), IL-1α (20–200ng/mL) and M5 cytokines cocktail (M5: TNF-α, Oncostatin M, IL-1α, IL-22, and IL-17A, each at 20 ng/mL), SIRT6 expression were not altered ( Supplementary fig 1A – C ). The increase in SIRT6 was caused by TNF-α stimulation, rather than other inflammatory factors. Therefore, in subsequent cell experiments, TNF-α at 40 ng/mL was used as the stimulatory concentration in HaCaT cells. Under this condition, the gene expression levels of various psoriasis-related inflammatory factors such as IL-1β, IL-6, IL-8, IL-23, TNF , as well as chemokines including CXCL1 and CCL20 , were elevated (). With the exception of SIRT6 , no significant changes were observed in the other members of the Sirtuins family (). To further investigate the role of SIRT6 in psoriasis, we overexpressed SIRT6 in HaCaT cells via lentiviral transfection. Compared with the blank control and lentiviral transfection control (NC), the SIRT6 overexpression (OE-SIRT6) exhibited significantly upregulated SIRT6 gene () and protein () levels. SIRT6 and the inflammatory factors IL-6, IL-23, TNF, S100A8 , and S100A9 exhibited increased gene expression upon TNF-α stimulation, and OE-SIRT6 further enhanced the TNF-α-induced gene expression of these factors (). Consistent with the gene changes, OE-SIRT6 promoted the secretion of the inflammatory factors IL-6 and IL-23 (). Overall, SIRT6 potentiated the TNF-α-induced inflammatory response in HaCaT cells.

To further explore the mechanism of SIRT6 in inflammation, we performed transcriptome sequencing on TNF-α-stimulated NC-HaCaT cells and OE-SIRT6 HaCaT cells. Compared with NC-HaCaT cells, OE-SIRT6 HaCaT cells stimulated with TNF-α exhibited 214 differentially expressed genes, including 97 up-regulated and 117 down-regulated genes (). Suppressor of cytokine signaling 2 (SOCS2) is a negative regulator of the JAK–STAT signaling pathway and inhibits the phosphorylation of STAT1, STAT3., OE-SIRT6 suppressed SOCS2 gene expression while enhancing the expression of STAT1, STAT2 , activator protein-1 genes (a downstream effector of JAK-STAT signaling, including JUN, FOS, FOSL1 ), inflammation-related genes ( IL1A, IL6ST, TNFRSF12A, TNFSF18, S100A9 ), and cell cycle–associated genes ( CDK1, CCNB1, CCND1, CCND2, CCND3 ) ( and ). In vitro experiments further confirmed that SIRT6 inhibited SOCS2 expression at both the gene and protein levels (). Moreover, OE-SIRT6 further enhanced TNF-α–induced phosphorylation of STAT1 and STAT3 ( and ). To corroborate these findings in vivo, we performed immunohistochemical staining of skin lesions from WT and SIRT6-Tg mice treated with or without imiquimod to induce psoriasis-like dermatitis. Consistent with the in vitro observations, SIRT6-Tg mice exhibited decreased SOCS2 expression and elevated STAT1 and STAT3 phosphorylation in the epidermis compared with WT mice ( Supplementary fig. 2A – D ), which was consistent with the exacerbated psoriatic phenotype upon SIRT6 overexpression. Thus, these findings suggested that SIRT6 might contribute to inflammatory responses by suppressing SOCS2 and sustaining STAT phosphorylation and activation.

Keratinocyte hyperproliferation is one of the key manifestations of psoriasis. Previous findings suggested an association between SIRT6 and cell proliferation (). Therefore, we investigated the effect of SIRT6 on HaCaT cells themselves. OE-SIRT6 accelerated HaCaT cell migration at 24 and 48 hours (), whereas SIRT6 knockdown had the opposite effect (). Moreover, OE-SIRT6 promoted HaCaT cell proliferation ().

To determine whether inhibition of SIRT6 could ameliorate inflammation, we transfected HaCaT cells with small interfering RNA to silence SIRT6 (si-SIRT6). All three siRNAs significantly suppressed SIRT6 expression ( and ). In subsequent experiments, we consistently used si-SIRT6-1 to knock down SIRT6 in HaCaT cells. Contrary to OE-SIRT6, si-SIRT6 suppressed the TNF-α-induced gene expression of SIRT6, IL-6, IL-23, TNF, S100A8 , and S100A9 (). Consistent with the changes in gene, si-SIRT6 inhibited the TNF-α-induced secretion of IL-6 and IL-23 by HaCaT cells (). In contrast to the effects of OE-SIRT6, si-SIRT6 upregulated SOCS2 protein levels and suppressed STAT1 and STAT3 phosphorylation (). Therefore, inhibiting SIRT6 suppressed the TNF-α-induced inflammatory response in HaCaT cells.

As the aforementioned in vitro experiments validated that inhibiting SIRT6 suppresses the inflammatory response, we proceeded to investigate whether inhibiting SIRT6 could ameliorate psoriasis-like symptoms in vivo. Hydrogel is a complex three-dimensional polymeric network with a semi-solid texture, excellent absorbency and biocompatibility. The unique structure of hydrogels is conducive to drug loading and release. Hydrogels are widely used in drug delivery, and studies have reported the topical application of hydrogels for delivering drugs to treat psoriasis., We incorporated OSS_128167, a potent selective SIRT6 inhibitor, into an alginate/carbomer-based hydrogel (OSS-gel). OSS-gel exhibits a certain viscosity and does not flow completely like a liquid (), which enables it to adhere better to skin compared to a solution. Under scanning electron microscopy (SEM), numerous loose pores were observed inside the OSS-gel, which facilitate drug storage (). Topical corticosteroids (TC) are one of the most commonly used and effective topical treatments for psoriasis and were used as a positive treatment control in our study. We applied Vaseline or IMQ to the ears of mice in the morning for 6 consecutive days. Eight hours later, the IMQ-treated mice were treated with vehicle-gel (Gel), OSS-gel, or TC, respectively. Compared to the IMQ group, the IMQ+OSS-gel group exhibited significant improvements in symptoms, as evidenced by markedly lower PSI scores and significantly reduced ear thickness, and this therapeutic effect was comparable to that of TC (). IMQ-induced modeling in mice led to weight loss, whereas OSS-gel treatment restored body weight to normal levels (), indicating the recovery of the overall health status in the mice. In addition to ameliorating dermatitis symptoms, OSS-gel treatment reduced the IMQ-induced enlargement of lymph nodes and spleen in mice (). OSS-gel reduced the IMQ-induced transcription level of SIRT6, IL-6, IL-23, TNF, S100A8 and S100A9 , and increased the level of SOCS2 in the ear skin tissue of mice (). Consistently, immunohistochemical analysis revealed that OSS-gel treatment promoted SOCS2 protein expression and suppressed STAT1 and STAT3 phosphorylation in the ear epidermis (). Collectively, these results indicated that topical OSS-gel exhibited anti-inflammatory efficacy comparable to TC, significantly ameliorating IMQ-induced psoriasiform dermatitis in mice.

To further evaluate the anti-inflammatory effect and clinical translation potential of OSS-gel, we assessed its efficacy in freshly obtained ex vivo psoriatic lesions from patients. The samples were divided into two equal pieces and cultured in 6-well plates containing complete medium at the air–liquid interface, with the epidermal surface facing upward. Vehicle hydrogel (vehicle-gel) or OSS-gel was topically applied to the surface of each lesion piece, respectively. After 24 hours of culture, RNA was extracted from the tissues and subjected to quantitative real-time PCR analysis (). OSS-gel inhibited the transcripts of SIRT6 , the pro-inflammatory markers IL-6, IL-23, S100A8, CXCL1, CXCL8, IL-1β and the Th17-related markers IL-17A, IL-17F and CCL20 while upregulating SOCS2 ; however, the decrease in S100A9 and TNF was not significant (, Supplementary fig. 3 ). These findings demonstrated that OSS-gel alleviated inflammatory responses in ex vivo psoriatic skin lesions, highlighting its therapeutic potential for clinical application in patients with psoriasis.
sections.discussion:
Our data identify SIRT6 as a positive regulator of keratinocyte-driven inflammation in psoriasis. SIRT6 expression was markedly upregulated in psoriatic epidermis and downregulated following effective treatment, suggesting that SIRT6 levels may serve as a molecular indicator of disease activity in psoriasis. Given that keratinocytes are central to psoriasis—not only as targets of inflammatory cytokines but also as active drivers that amplify cutaneous inflammation through production of cytokines, alarmins, and chemokines that recruit and activate immune cells —we focused on the keratinocyte-intrinsic functions of SIRT6. Notably, TNF-α stimulation directly induced SIRT6 in HaCaT cells in a dose-dependent manner, indicating that the inflammatory milieu itself may perpetuate SIRT6 upregulation in lesional keratinocytes. Functionally, SIRT6 overexpression amplified TNF-α-induced production of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-23, TNF-α) and alarmins (S100A8, S100A9), while also promoting keratinocyte proliferation and migration—two hallmarks of psoriatic keratinocyte abnormality. Conversely, SIRT6 knockdown reversed these pro-inflammatory effects. These gain- and loss-of-function data establish a causal role for SIRT6 in driving a pathogenic keratinocyte phenotype that likely contributes to the amplification and maintenance of psoriasiform inflammation.

Mechanistically, our data suggest a potential involvement of the SOCS2–STAT1/3 axis in SIRT6-mediated inflammation. SIRT6 overexpression suppressed SOCS2 expression at both mRNA and protein levels, concomitantly enhancing STAT1 and STAT3 phosphorylation, whereas SIRT6 knockdown or pharmacological inhibition restored SOCS2 and attenuated STAT1/3 phosphorylation across cellular, animal, and ex vivo psoriatic lesional models. Given that SOCS proteins are canonical negative regulators of JAK/STAT signaling that bind to JAKs via their SH2 domains and competitively inhibit STAT activation, our findings suggest that SIRT6 relieves this physiological brake on STAT1/3 signaling by suppressing SOCS2. This regulatory relationship closely resembles a previous study showing that SIRT6 suppresses SOCS3 transcription in intestinal epithelial cells through histone H3K56 deacetylation, thereby promoting STAT6 phosphorylation. It is therefore plausible that SIRT6 may regulate SOCS2 transcription through a similar epigenetic mechanism in keratinocytes. However, several questions remain. First, whether SIRT6 directly binds to the SOCS2 promoter and modulates its transcriptional activity via histone deacetylation requires formal demonstration by chromatin immunoprecipitation. Second, whether SOCS2 restoration is sufficient to attenuate STAT1/3 hyperphosphorylation and the associated inflammatory phenotype warrants functional rescue experiments. Future studies incorporating these approaches will help to define the precise molecular circuitry linking SIRT6 to SOCS2–STAT1/3 signaling. Nevertheless, our gain- and loss-of-function data collectively establish that SIRT6 promotes psoriatic inflammation, at least in part, through downregulation of SOCS2 and consequent hyperactivation of STAT1/3, supporting the notion that targeting SIRT6 may offer a therapeutic opportunity for psoriasis.

Novel transdermal drug delivery systems, including hydrogels and nanogels, have emerged as a current research hotspot in the development of topical therapies for skin diseases, with hydrogels being particularly favored for their ease of application and high biocompatibility. In addition to its use in psoriasis, it has been previously reported for the treatment of diabetes-related foot ulcers, skin infections, burn injuries, androgenic alopecia. In our study, OSS-gel demonstrated comparable efficacy to TC in the IMQ-induced mouse model, with significant improvements observed in PSI scores, ear thickness, histopathological features, and inflammatory cytokine expression. At the molecular level, OSS-gel treatment upregulated SOCS2 expression and suppressed STAT1/3 phosphorylation in IMQ-treated mouse epidermis, consistent with our in vitro mechanistic findings. Furthermore, OSS-gel exerted consistent anti-inflammatory effects in ex vivo psoriatic lesions, downregulating multiple psoriasis-related inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, including IL-6, IL-23, IL-17A, IL-17F, CCL20 , etc, across three patient specimens. Although the sample size is limited, the observed anti-inflammatory trend was consistent and pronounced. Given that SIRT6 has been reported to promote IL-17A transcription by deacetylating RORγt and enhancing its binding to the IL-17A promoter, it is plausible that OSS-gel may attenuate IL-17 transcription through this pathway, while the broader therapeutic potential of OSS-gel in Th17 cell modulation and the prevention of psoriasis recurrence warrants further investigation.

Several limitations of our study should be acknowledged. First, the IMQ-induced mouse model, as the most widely used and conveniently established murine model for psoriasis, represents an acute TLR7/8-driven inflammatory response rather than the chronic, relapsing nature of human psoriasis. This model does not recapitulate the T-cell memory or the recurrent disease flares that characterize clinical psoriasis, and therefore cannot address the potential of OSS-gel in disease prevention or long-term management. Second, the number of ex vivo human skin specimens was limited (n=3), and although the anti-inflammatory effects were consistent across samples, the small sample size precludes definitive conclusions about patient heterogeneity. These preliminary data, however, provide a rationale for sample size estimation in future clinical trials and support further development of OSS-gel as a potential alternative topical therapy for psoriasis.

Our findings show that SIRT6 overexpression correlates with reduced SOCS2 expression and increased STAT1/3 phosphorylation, whereas SIRT6 inhibition produces the opposite molecular and anti-inflammatory effects. Collectively, these results position SIRT6 as a promising therapeutic target for psoriasis, and our hydrogel-based inhibitor delivery system highlights its translational potential.
