sections.results:
Guselkumab inhibits the interaction of IL-23 with its receptor by selectively binding to its p19 subunit, thereby blocking IL-23-dependent cell signalling and proinflammatory cytokine release [, ]. Guselkumab has been shown to reduce serum IL-17A, IL-17F and IL-22 levels in adults with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis and those with active psoriatic arthritis, and serum C-reactive protein, amyloid A and IL-6 levels in adults with active psoriatic arthritis relative to pre-treatment levels; however, the relationship between these pharmacodynamic markers and the mechanism(s) by which guselkumab exerts its clinical effects is not yet known [, ].

In pediatric patients ≥ 6 years of age and weighing ≥ 40 kg with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis, steady-state serum trough guselkumab concentrations were achieved by week 20 and were within the range of those seen in both adults with plaque psoriasis and adults with psoriatic arthritis [, ]. At week 16 of the 16-week placebo-controlled period of the phase III PROTOSTAR study (Sect. ), mean serum guselkumab concentrations were 2.83 µg/mL and 3.61 µg/mL in patients ≥ 6 to < 12 years of age and ≥ 12 to < 18 years of age, respectively, and 3.53 µg/mL and 3.19 µg/mL in those with a baseline weight of < 70 kg and ≥ 70 kg, respectively [, ]. In parts 1 and 2 of PROTOSTAR, with each part extending over 52 weeks, mean steady-state serum guselkumab concentrations were reached at week 20 (1.11 µg/mL and 1.52 µg/mL, respectively) and maintained through week 44 [, ].

As a human IgG monoclonal antibody, guselkumab is expected to be degraded into small peptides and amino acids by catabolic pathways []. According to population pharmacokinetic analyses, the concomitant use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, oral corticosteroids and conventional DMARDs did not affect the clearance of guselkumab. There is low potential for clinically relevant drug interactions between guselkumab and drugs metabolized by CYP3A4, CYP2C9, CYP2C19 and CYP1A2 in patients with moderate-to-severe psoriasis, but interaction potential with drugs metabolized by CYP2D6 cannot be ruled out [].

In the randomized, placebo-controlled, multinational phase III PROTOSTAR ( NCT03451851 ; PsO5) study in pediatric patients ≥ 6 to < 18 years of age with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis, treatment with guselkumab administered by subcutaneous injection resulted in statistically significant and clinically meaningful improvements in validated measures of plaque psoriasis severity compared with placebo [].

The main PROTOSTAR study comprises two parts []. Part 1 consists of a 16-week placebo-controlled period followed by a 36-week period in which treatment with guselkumab was withdrawn and restarted, continued, or initiated depending on whether the patient achieved a ≥ 90% improvement from baseline in Psoriasis Area and Severity Index score (PASI 90) at week 16 and their initial treatment assignment. Patients ≥ 12 to < 18 years of age and those ≥ 6 to < 12 years of age were randomized to part 1(a) and part 1(b), respectively, to receive guselkumab, placebo or etanercept. In part 2, patients ≥ 12 to < 18 years of age received continuous open-label treatment with guselkumab over the course of a 52-week period. Following completion of parts 1 or 2, patients could continue to receive weight-based guselkumab treatment every 8 weeks in an open-label long-term extension phase. In the main study, the co-primary endpoints in part 1 outside the USA were the proportion of patients achieving an Investigator Global Assessment score of 0/1 (IGA 0/1) and the proportion of patients achieving a ≥ 75% improvement in PASI score (PASI 75) at week 16, while those required by the US FDA were the proportion of patients achieving IGA 0/1 response and the proportion of patients achieving PASI 90 response at week 16. The proportion of patients achieving PASI 90 response at week 16 of part 1 was a major secondary endpoint outside the USA while the proportion of patients achieving PASI 75 response at week 16 of part 1 was a US FDA-required major secondary endpoint. Other major secondary endpoints assessed at week 16 of part 1 were the proportions of patients achieving IGA score of 0 (i.e. clear skin) and 100% improvement in PASI score (PASI 100), and the change from baseline in the validated Children’s Dermatology Life Quality Index (CDLQI) questionnaire score [].

At week 16 of PROTOSTAR part 1, all co-primary and major secondary endpoints were met []. A significantly higher proportion of guselkumab recipients than placebo recipients achieved IGA 0/1 [66% of 41 patients vs 16% of 25 patients; treatment difference 50 (95% CI 26–69); p < 0.001], PASI 75 [76% vs 20%; treatment difference 56 (95% CI 32–74); p < 0.001], PASI 90 [56% vs 16%; treatment difference 40 (95% CI 16–61); p = 0.003], IGA 0 (39% vs 4%; p = 0.004) and PASI 100 (34% vs 0%; p = 0.002) responses at week 16. The least-squares mean improvement from baseline in CDLQI score (scores range from 0–30, with higher scores indicating greater impact on quality of life) at week 16 was significantly greater in patients receiving guselkumab than those receiving placebo (– 7.3 vs. – 1.9; p < 0.001). In the part 1 open-label etanercept (active reference) arm, 69%, 69% and 54% of 26 patients achieved IGA 0/1, PASI 75 and PASI 90 responses, respectively, at week 16. At the end of the 16-week placebo-controlled period, 23 (56%) guselkumab recipients who achieved PASI 90 response were withdrawn from guselkumab, 18 (44%) guselkumab recipients were PASI 90 nonresponders continued to receive guselkumab and 20 (80%) placebo recipients were PASI 90 nonresponders who crossed over to receive guselkumab for the remainder of part 1 (i.e. 36 weeks). Moreover, 22 (85%) of 26 etanercept recipients crossed over to receive guselkumab at week 20 for the remainder of part 1 (i.e. 32 weeks) [].

At week 52 of PROTOSTAR part 1, improvements in response rates from week 16 were seen in the 20 patients previously randomized to placebo who crossed over to receive guselkumab (IGA 0/1, PASI 75 and PASI 90 response rates, respectively were 0%, 5% and 0% at week 16 and 80%, 95% and 65% at week 52) and the 22 patients previously randomized to etanercept who crossed over to receive guselkumab (IGA 0/1, PASI 75 and PASI 90 response rates, respectively were 64%, 55% and 36% at week 20 and 91%, 96% and 91% at week 52) []. PASI 90 response was achieved at week 52 by 61% of the 18 guselkumab recipients who were PASI 90 nonresponders at week 16 and continued to receive guselkumab [].

For the 23 patients who achieved PASI 90 response at week 16 and were withdrawn from guselkumab, the median time to losing PASI 90 response was 24 weeks []. Almost one-third (30%) of these 23 patients maintained the PASI 90 response at week 52. Four of the patients who lost PASI 90 response were eligible (defined as a ≥ 50% loss of the PASI improvement achieved by week 16) for retreatment: two were retreated at week 44 and two at week 48. At week 52, one of two evaluable patients had regained PASI 90 response [].

In PROTOSTAR part 2, 28 patients ≥ 12 to < 18 years of age initiated open-label treatment with guselkumab, with 27 receiving treatment through 52 weeks []. At week 16 of part 2, IGA 0/1, PASI 75, PASI 90, IGA 0 and PASI 100 responses were achieved by 89%, 82%, 64%, 46% and 36% of patients, respectively. At week 52, the respective responses were achieved by 86%, 93%, 82%, 75% and 54% of patients, and the mean change from baseline in CDLQI was – 7.3 [].

Patients eligible for PROTOSTAR had been diagnosed with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis for ≥ 6 months (with or without psoriatic arthritis); had IGA score of ≥ 3 [scores range from 0 (clear skin) to 4 (severe disease)]; had PASI score of ≥ 12 (scores range from 0–72, with higher scores indicating greater disease severity); and had ≥ 10% body surface area (BSA) involvement []. Participants were also required to have ≥ 1 of the following: very thick lesions, clinically relevant facial, genital or hand/foot involvement, PASI score of ≥ 20, > 20% BSA involvement, or IGA score of 4. Eligible patients were candidates for phototherapy/systemic therapy and had disease inadequately controlled by phototherapy and/or topical therapy. Exclusion criteria included non-plaque/drug-induced psoriasis, a history of chronic/recurrent infectious disease or lymphoproliferative disease, and the use of systemic therapies that could affect plaque psoriasis or IGA evaluation within 2 weeks of initiating the study drug [].

In the 16-week placebo-controlled period of part 1, guselkumab and placebo were administered by subcutaneous injection in a double-blind and weight-based (1.3 mg/kg and 100 mg for those weighing < 70 kg and ≥ 70 kg, respectively) manner at weeks 0, 4 and 12, while etanercept (serving as a reference treatment for clinical response only) was administered by subcutaneous injection in an open-label and weight-based (0.8 mg/kg up to 50 mg per dose) manner once weekly through week 15 []. Guselkumab and placebo were administered via subcutaneous injection using a single-use prefilled syringe (which delivered a single fixed dose of 100 mg) or one or two prefilled pen(s) [each of which delivered a dose of up to 45 mg]. At week 16, guselkumab treatment was withdrawn from recipients who had achieved PASI 90 response; patients restarted guselkumab only if they experienced ≥ 50% loss in the PASI improvement achieved by week 16 (with injections administered at the visit at which the loss of improvement was identified, 4 weeks later and then every 8 weeks thereafter through week 52). Guselkumab recipients who had not achieved PASI 90 response at week 16 continued receiving treatment with guselkumab every 8 weeks through week 52 (although they received placebo at week 16 to maintain study blinding). Among placebo recipients who had achieved PASI 90 response at week 16, guselkumab therapy was initiated only following a ≥ 50% loss in the PASI improvement achieved by week 16 (with injections administered at the visit at which the loss of improvement was identified, 4 weeks later and then every 8 weeks thereafter through week 52). Placebo recipients who had not achieved PASI 90 response at week 16 crossed over to receive guselkumab at weeks 16 and 20 and then every 8 weeks through week 52. At week 16, etanercept recipients had the option to switch to receiving guselkumab at weeks 20, 24 and every 8 weeks thereafter through week 52 or discontinue treatment at week 16. In part 2, patients received guselkumab in an open-label manner at weeks 0 and 4 and then every 8 weeks through week 52 [].

In part 1, at baseline, 67% and 33% of 92 patients were 12 to < 18 years of age and ≥ 6 to < 12 years of age, respectively []. In the overall population, the mean PASI score was 18.8; mean BSA involvement was 24%; 78% and 22% of patients had IGA score of 3 or 4, respectively; and the mean CDLQI score was 9.4. All patients had previously used topical therapy and 39% had used systemic therapy. In part 2, at baseline, the mean PASI score was 21.2; mean BSA involvement was 29%; 54% and 46% of patients had IGA scores of 3 and 4, respectively; and the mean CDLQI score was 8.3. All patients had previously used topical therapy and 50% had used systemic therapy [].

The clinical presentation of psoriatic arthritis in pediatric patients overlaps that of psoriatic arthritis in adults, plaque psoriasis in pediatric patients and plaque psoriasis in adults []. This, along with comparable pharmacokinetic, clinical response and safety data in these populations, supports the extrapolation of guselkumab efficacy and safety data from adult patients with psoriatic arthritis and pediatric and adult patients with plaque psoriasis to pediatric patients with psoriatic arthritis []. Data from 494 and 727 adults with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis in VOYAGE 1 [] and VOYAGE 2 [], respectively; 127 and 248 adults with active psoriatic arthritis in DISCOVER 1 [] and DISCOVER 2 [], respectively; and 92 pediatric patients with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis in PROTOSTAR (3 of whom had concomitant psoriatic arthritis) [] who received guselkumab every 8 weeks, were included in this analysis [].

Serum guselkumab concentrations were similar between pediatric patients with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis (maximum observed median 3.2 µg/mL at week 16) and adults with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis (maximum median 3.7 µg/mL at week 8), between adults with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis (median 1.0–3.7 µg/mL) and those with active psoriatic arthritis (median 1.0–3.1 µg/mL), and between pediatric patients with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis (maximum observed median 3.2 µg/mL at week 16), with or without psoriatic arthritis, and adults with active psoriatic arthritis (maximum observed median 4.2 µg/mL at week 2) [].

Skin disease improvements were comparable across the assessed patient populations []. At week 16, IGA 0/1 response was achieved by 66% of pediatric patients with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis, 85% of adults with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis and 77% of adults with active psoriatic arthritis. At the same timepoint, PASI 75/90/100 responses, respectively, were achieved by 77%, 56% and 33% of pediatric patients with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis (but without psoriatic arthritis), 88%, 71%, and 35% of adults with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis, and 77%, 55% and 22% of adults with active psoriatic arthritis [].

Baseline characteristics in the patient groups analyzed were generally comparable apart from age and duration of disease, and were consistent with previously reported study populations [].

In pediatric patients ≥ 6 to < 18 years of age with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis participating in PROTOSTAR, the safety profile of guselkumab was similar to that of placebo and consistent with the established safety profile of the drug in adults with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis [, ]. No new safety signals were identified []. Moreover, safety outcomes with guselkumab therapy were similar across pediatric and adult patients, as well as psoriatic indications: close alignment was seen between pediatric patients with plaque psoriasis who did ( n = 3) or did not ( n = 89) have psoriatic arthritis [].

In the PROTOSTAR 16-week placebo-controlled period, ≥ 1 adverse event (AE) occurred in 42% of 41 guselkumab recipients and 68% of 25 placebo recipients, with ≥ 1 infection reported in 29% and 40% of patients, respectively []. The most frequently reported AEs (occurring in > 5% of patients in the guselkumab group and with a numerically higher incidence than the placebo group) were upper respiratory tract infection (URTI) [10% vs 8%] and headache (7% vs 0%). One patient in each group experienced a mild injection-site reaction (ISR). One serious AE (a radius fracture that was considered unrelated to the study treatment) was reported in the guselkumab group, and one AE resulting in discontinuation (worsening psoriasis) was reported in the placebo group during the placebo-controlled period. No case of active tuberculosis, opportunistic infections or malignancy occurred and no patient died. In the etanercept group, one patient experienced ISRs through week 16 [].

Through week 52 of PROTOSTAR part 1, ≥ 1 AE occurred in 72% of 86 guselkumab recipients (80% of 41 patients originally randomized to guselkumab, 70% of 23 patients originally randomized to placebo who crossed over to guselkumab, and 59% of 22 patients originally randomized to etanercept who crossed over to guselkumab, with patients in the respective groups having received a total of 52 weeks, 36 weeks and 32 weeks of treatment with guselkumab) []. At least one infection was reported in 58% (61%, 52% and 59%, respectively) of guselkumab-treated patients. The most frequently reported AEs (occurring in > 5% of patients) were nasopharyngitis (28% of patients), URTI (13%), headache (12%) and pharyngitis (6%). ISRs (all mild) were reported in 2% of patients. One serious AE (chronic tonsillitis in a patient originally randomized to placebo that was considered unrelated to the study treatment) and one treatment discontinuation (pregnancy in a patient originally randomized to guselkumab) occurred. No case of active tuberculosis, opportunistic infections or malignancy occurred, and no patient died [].

In PROTOSTAR part 2, the rates and types of observed AEs in the 28 patients ≥ 12 to < 18 years of age who initiated therapy with open-label guselkumab were similar to those seen in part 1 []. Through week 52 of part 2, ≥ 1 AE and ≥ 1 infection occurred in 82% and 54% of patients, respectively. The most frequently reported AEs (occurring in > 5% of patients) were nasopharyngitis (25% of patients), URTI (7%) and headache (7%). ISRs (all mild) were reported in 7% of patients. One serious AE (trauma due to a fall that was considered unrelated to the study treatment) and one treatment discontinuation (suicidal ideation) occurred. No case of active tuberculosis, opportunistic infections or malignancy occurred, and no patient died [].

From the first dose of guselkumab through week 44 in PROTOSTAR, 18% of 114 evaluable pediatric patients ≥ 6 years of age tested positive for guselkumab antidrug antibodies (ADAs) with generally low titres; none of the ADA-positive patients developed neutralizing ADAs []. Consistent with previous observations in adults, ADAs had no effect on the pharmacokinetics, safety of and the clinical response to guselkumab in pediatric patients [].

Recruitment is underway for four multinational phase III studies that will assess the efficacy and/or safety of guselkumab in patients 5–17 years of age with active juvenile psoriatic arthritis ( NCT05083182 ; PSUMMIT Jr); those 2–17 years of age with moderately to severely active Crohn’s disease ( NCT05923073 ; MACARONI-23); those 2–17 years of age with moderately to severely active ulcerative colitis ( NCT06260163 ; QUASAR Jr); and a long-term extension in patients ≥ 3 years of age with Crohn's disease, juvenile psoriatic arthritis and ulcerative colitis ( NCT06663332 ; TRILOGY).

Guselkumab received its first pediatric approvals on 26 September 2025 for the treatment of pediatric patients 6 years of age and older and weighing ≥ 40 kg who either have moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis and are candidates for systemic therapy or phototherapy, or who have active psoriatic arthritis [, ]. Subsequently, guselkumab was approved on 18 December 2025 in the EU for the treatment of moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis in children and adolescents from the age of 6 years who are candidates for systemic therapy [, ].

title: Real-World Effectiveness and Safety of Ixekizumab in Moderate-to-Severe Plaque Psoriasis in the Indian Population: A Pilot Study.
abstract: BackgroundIndia has a significant burden of psoriasis, with an incidence reported between 0.44% and 2.2% among total dermatology patients and a reported prevalence of 4.78% over 5 years. Psoriasis is now recognized as a multisystem disease, and targeted therapies are needed to reduce morbidity. The need for newer biologics exists not only for better disease control but also to treat patients who manifest primary or secondary failure to a previous biologic. Ixekizumab is a newer IL-17 inhibitor that has recently been approved by the Drug Controller General of India for use in patients with psoriasis vulgaris in India.Aims and objectivesTo evaluate the effectiveness and safety of ixekizumab in the treatment of patients with plaque psoriasis of Indian origin.Patients and methodsThe study was a prospective, single-center, single-arm interventional study approved prospectively by Clinical Trial Registry-India with reg. no. CTRI/2025/02/081205. The induction phase of ixekizumab was used to treat 40 patients with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis. The psoriasis area severity index (PASI), body surface area (BSA), and dermatology life quality index (DLQI) were measured at 2, 4, and 12 weeks of therapy. Median values of absolute PASI and BSA were assessed statistically using the Friedman test and Wilcoxon-signed rank test. PASI 75/90/100 responses were measured at 2, 4, and 12 weeks and analyzed using Cochran's Q test and McNemar test. Safety and adverse events, if any, were documented.ResultsThe median absolute PASI, BSA, and DLQI showed progressive improvement during the study period and these values when compared between baseline and 12 weeks were statistically significant. PASI 75/90/100 at the end of 12 weeks was 100%, 75%, and 20%, respectively. All eleven patients who had primary or secondary failure to a previous biologic showed a comparable response to that achieved by biologic naïve patients. No major adverse events were noted.LimitationsConsidering that it is a pilot study which concluded in the induction phase of the treatment, long-term treatment outcomes and adverse events cannot be commented upon.ConclusionIxekizumab achieved high PASI targets during the induction phase. The treatment improved the DLQI significantly. It has an excellent safety profile in the Indian population. Its effectiveness in patients with previous biologic failure is comparable to that in biologic naïve patients.

sections.abstract:
India has a significant burden of psoriasis, with an incidence reported between 0.44% and 2.2% among total dermatology patients and a reported prevalence of 4.78% over 5 years. Psoriasis is now recognized as a multisystem disease, and targeted therapies are needed to reduce morbidity. The need for newer biologics exists not only for better disease control but also to treat patients who manifest primary or secondary failure to a previous biologic. Ixekizumab is a newer IL-17 inhibitor that has recently been approved by the Drug Controller General of India for use in patients with psoriasis vulgaris in India.

To evaluate the effectiveness and safety of ixekizumab in the treatment of patients with plaque psoriasis of Indian origin.

The study was a prospective, single-center, single-arm interventional study approved prospectively by Clinical Trial Registry-India with reg. no. CTRI/2025/02/081205. The induction phase of ixekizumab was used to treat 40 patients with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis. The psoriasis area severity index (PASI), body surface area (BSA), and dermatology life quality index (DLQI) were measured at 2, 4, and 12 weeks of therapy. Median values of absolute PASI and BSA were assessed statistically using the Friedman test and Wilcoxon-signed rank test. PASI 75/90/100 responses were measured at 2, 4, and 12 weeks and analyzed using Cochran’s Q test and McNemar test. Safety and adverse events, if any, were documented.

The median absolute PASI, BSA, and DLQI showed progressive improvement during the study period and these values when compared between baseline and 12 weeks were statistically significant. PASI 75/90/100 at the end of 12 weeks was 100%, 75%, and 20%, respectively. All eleven patients who had primary or secondary failure to a previous biologic showed a comparable response to that achieved by biologic naïve patients. No major adverse events were noted.

Considering that it is a pilot study which concluded in the induction phase of the treatment, long-term treatment outcomes and adverse events cannot be commented upon.

Ixekizumab achieved high PASI targets during the induction phase. The treatment improved the DLQI significantly. It has an excellent safety profile in the Indian population. Its effectiveness in patients with previous biologic failure is comparable to that in biologic naïve patients.

Keywords: Biologic , ixekizumab , newer IL-17 inhibitor , plaque psoriasis
sections.other:
India has a significant burden of psoriasis , with reported incidence between 0.44% and 2.2% among total skin patients and prevalence being 4.78% over 5 years.[]

In the last two decades, biologic therapies have revolutionized the treatment of most dermatologic diseases, including plaque psoriasis. With increasing demand for better treatment outcomes and improved quality of life, these targeted therapies are becoming more popular. Approved biologics for psoriasis include tumor necrosis factor inhibitors (TNFi), interleukin-17A inhibitors (IL-17i), interleukin-12/23 inhibitors (IL-12/23i), and interleukin-23 inhibitors (IL-23i).[,] There is a continuing need for newer molecules that can achieve faster and sustained outcomes, with minimal to no adverse events compared to the currently available options. These molecules should also be able to treat patients who have had primary or secondary treatment failures to previous biologics and now require switching. Ixekizumab is one such newer molecule.

Ixekizumab is an IgG4 monoclonal antibody that selectively targets and binds IL-17A, with very high affinity.[] The Food and Drug Administration and European Medicines Agency approved the molecule in 2016 for treating patients with moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis.[] Since then, various studies have highlighted the molecule’s faster onset of action and good safety profile, including the UNCOVER- 3 study by Blauvelt et al .[] Most of the available trials and studies have been funded by the manufacturing or marketing company.[] By observing outcomes in diverse populations and environments, real-world studies offer valuable information on effectiveness, safety, and practical implications.

Certain differences in the efficacy of biologics exists in different ethnic groups. Biologic agents such as secukinumab, brodalumab and ixekizumab have been studied to have superior efficacy in non-white racial/ethnic group.[] Studies in Chinese and White psoriasis patients with HLA-Cw*06 showed a greater, faster, and longer duration of response to ustekinumab, highlighting the role of pharmacogenetics.[] Studies from Indian (skin of color) patients regarding the efficacy and safety of ixekizumab in treating moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis are lacking.

We studied this molecule at our tertiary care hospital to evaluate the drug’s effectiveness and safety during treatment of psoriatic patients of Indian origin. We also assessed its response in patients who have experienced primary or secondary biologic treatment failure. This is a pioneer work restricted to the induction phase, i.e. till 12 weeks; however, the molecule continues to be studied for long-term treatment outcome at our center.

Dr. Vishal Sharma, Assistant Prof PSM, Army College Of Medical Sciences, New Delhi for technical support including statistical analysis.

Nil.

This was a prospective, single-center, single-arm, interventional study conducted in the dermatology department of Base Hospital Delhi Cantt, New Delhi, which is a tertiary care teaching hospital and medical college. The study was designed in September 2024, following the recent approval of ixekizumab by Drug Controller General of India for use in India (March 2023).

Drug procurement was arranged through the hospital medical stores, which provide free biologic treatment to all entitled patients. Permission from the institutional ethics committee (full committee) was obtained in October 2024 (reg. no. IEC-05/2024/04).

The study was registered with the Clinical Trial Registry-India (ICMR-NIMS), and approvals were received in February 2025 (reg. no. CTRI/2025/02/081205); following which, patients were recruited, and the study was conducted. Written informed consent in the patients’ language was obtained from all participants.

This was a pilot study, and thus a small sample size was selected. The study population included 40 patients with plaque psoriasis above the age of 18 years, with psoriasis area severity index (PASI), body surface area (BSA), and dermatology life quality index (DLQI) scores greater than 10, with or without involvement of the palms and soles, nails, or joints. These included patients who were biologic naïve as well as those who had failed a previous biologic or any other immunosuppressant. Criteria for primary failure were taken as insufficient response (patients not achieving PASI 50) at week 12, and criteria for secondary failure included loss of response (PASI > 50% of the initial value) in a patient who had previously achieved PASI 50 at week 12.[,]

Exclusion criteria included patients with subgroups having isolated nail psoriasis, palmoplantar psoriasis, pustular psoriasis, inverse psoriasis, and psoriatic arthritis. Patients with irritable bowel disease, active tuberculosis, pregnancy, lactating females, malignancy, active infections, and drug hypersensitivity were also excluded from the study.

Statistical analysis was done using the statistical package for the social sciences version 21.0. Categorical variables, including age, gender, presence of nail, palmoplantar, or joint psoriasis, comorbidities, LTBI status, prior biologic experience, and reason for switching to ixekizumab, were summarized using percentages.

Continuous variables, such as means, standard deviations, and the 25 th , 50 th (median), and 75 th percentiles of PASI, BSA, and DLQI, were tabulated at baseline, 2, 4, and 12 weeks.

As response outcome was measured at four different time frames, two nonparametric tests, namely Friedman and Wilcoxon signed-rank test, were used to analyze the values of PASI, BSA, and DLQI at these time points. P value and z -score were used to indicate significance in the outcomes of PASI, BSA, and DLQI after treatment. Normality of BSA, PASI, and DLQI was checked at all intervals using Kolmogorov–Smirnov and Shapiro–Wilk tests.

PASI 75/90/100 responses were also calculated at 2, 4, and 12 weeks using a yes/no analysis and expressed as percentages. To evaluate whether response rates differed across the three time points, Cochran’s Q test was conducted. Upon finding a significant Cochran’s Q test, post hoc pairwise comparisons were performed using McNemar’s test to examine differences between each pair of time points. To control for Type I error due to multiple comparisons, a Bonferroni correction was applied, setting the significance threshold at P < 0.017 (0.05/3). All tests were two-tailed, and P values less than 0.05 were considered statistically significant unless otherwise adjusted.

Thus, both absolute PASI and PASI 75/90/100 were used to assess the response to therapy. There were no treatment dropouts, and thus no attrition rates.

The datasets generated and/or analysed during the current study are not publicly available as they include patient details, but are available from the corresponding author on reasonble request.
sections.methods:
The study population was evaluated for demographic profile, presence of nail, palmoplantar, or joint psoriasis, comorbidities, latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI) status, prior biologic experience, and reason for switching to ixekizumab. All patients underwent baseline laboratory tests, viral markers, and interferon gamma release assay (IGRA). Patients who were IGRA positive were further investigated to rule out active tuberculosis and were treated adequately before starting ixekizumab.

All prior medications, both oral and topical, including immunosuppressants, were discontinued at the start of treatment. All patients had high disease activity and were therefore shifted to ixekizumab from previous treatment (disease modifying anti rheumatic drug/biologic) immediately, without waiting for wash out period to prevent acute exacerbation of psoriasis. Patients were advised to take levocetirizine 5 mg on a need basis during the study, for pruritus on psoriatic lesions.

The study population was treated with subcutaneous injections of ixekizumab, supplied as a prefilled syringe containing 80 mg. A standard dose of 160 mg at week 0, followed by 80 mg every 2 weeks until week 12, was used during the induction phase. PASI, BSA, and DLQI were measured for all patients at baseline and during follow-up visits at 2, 4, and 12 weeks. A smartphone-based PASI calculator (MD + CALC by Dr. Torsten Friedriksson) was used consistently for PASI calculation at all time points. PASI results from the calculator were rechecked manually. BSA was measured clinically by the Wallace’s rule of nine assessment tool. The DLQI questionnaire was reciprocated in the patients’ language by the principal investigator (PI) and scored.

Hemogram, liver and kidney function tests were repeated at 2, 4, and 12 weeks to assess for any side effects of treatment. Patients were instructed to report any adverse events after the administration of the injection directly to the PI via telephone or during follow-up visits.
sections.results:
The mean age of the patients was 43.4 years. Of the 40 patients, 22 (55%) were male and 18 (45%) were female. In addition to plaque psoriasis, three (7.5%) patients had palmoplantar involvement, five (12.5%) had nail involvement, and two (5%) had psoriatic arthritis. Fourteen patients (35%) had a known comorbidity, the most common being metabolic syndrome; one patient was a special child with Down syndrome. Six patients (15%) had LTBI [].

Fifteen patients (37.5%) had prior experience with biologics [secukinumab: 9 (60%), adalimumab: 4 (26.66%), etanercept: 1 (6.66%), and infliximab: 1 (6.66%)]. Reasons for switching to ixekizumab included secondary failure (8, 53.33%), primary failure (3, 20%), adverse events to biologics (2, 13.33%), and treatment dropouts (2, 13.33%) during remission. Twenty five patients (62.5%) were biologic naïve [].

The median absolute PASI and interquartile range (IQR) at baseline, 2, 4, and 12 weeks of treatment was 29.75 (20-38.75), 9.25 (6.5-12.45), 4.6 (3-6), and 1.8 (1-3.15), respectively. A Friedman test showed a P < 0.001, which was statistically significant. The median BSA and IQR at baseline, 2, 4, and 12 weeks were 35.5 (25.5–45), 18.5 (12–25.75), 9 (6–13.75), and 4 (1–5), respectively, and a Friedman test showed a P < 0.001, which was statistically significant. The median DLQI and IQR at baseline, 2, 4, and 12 weeks were 17.4 (14–19), 5 (4–6), 3 (2–3.75), and 1 (1–2), respectively, and a Friedman test showed a P < 0.001, which was statistically significant []. Wilcoxon signed-rank test scores for PASI, BSA, and DLQI showed consistent negative rank and statistically significant results across all compared intervals of treatment [].

The mean values of PASI, BSA, and DLQI at baseline, 2, 4, and 12 weeks after treatment with ixekizumab are graphically represented in .

PASI 75/90/100 responses at 2 weeks were achieved by 10%, 0%, and 0% patients; at 4 weeks were achieved by 82.5%, 20%, and 0% patients; and at 12 weeks were achieved by 100%, 75%, and 20% patients, respectively. The Null hypothesis showed that the distributions of PASI 75/90/100 at 2, 4, and 12 weeks were similar. Cochran’s Q test, when applied to the related samples of PASI (75/90/100) at 2, 4, and 12 weeks, showed P values of. 0.018, 0.00, 0.00, respectively, which were statistically significant. Post hoc pairwise McNemar tests with Bonferroni correction revealed significant increases in response rates between study intervals for PASI 75/90/100 [].

Patients with secukinumab failure had median absolute PASI and IQR values of 26.5 (15–45), 10.95 (5.7–13), 4.5 (3–7.5), and 2.5 (0–3.5) at baseline and at 2, 4, and 12 weeks, respectively. Among these patients, PASI 75/90/100 responses at 2 weeks were achieved by 0%, 0%, and 0% patients; at 4 weeks by 66.67%, 16.66%, and 0% patients; and at 12 weeks by 100%, 50%, and 33.34% patients, respectively.

Patients with TNFi (adalimumab and etanercept) failure had median absolute PASI and IQR values of 38 (21.1–42.5), 12 (6–20), 5 (2.8–11.1), and 2 (0.5–5) at baseline and at 2, 4, and 12 weeks, respectively. Among adalimumab failures, PASI 75/90/100 responses at 2 weeks were achieved by 0%, 0%, and 0% patients; at 4 weeks by 80%, 20%, and 0% of patients; and at 12 weeks by 100%, 80%, and 20% of patients, respectively.

At follow-up visits, no significant clinical improvement was observed in either nail or palmoplantar lesions; however, these were not assessed separately by a different scoring system, which did not impact the outcome of our study. All patients with psoriatic arthritis remained symptom-free and showed no disease activity, but improvement was not graded.

Treatment with ixekizumab demonstrated an excellent safety profile, with no major side effects of interest noted over 12 weeks. However, three (7.5%) patients experienced mild-to-moderate itching on psoriatic lesions a few hours after the first dose of ixekizumab (160 mg). This was managed with antihistamines for 5 days, resulting in complete resolution of symptoms and no recurrences with subsequent doses. Laboratory profiles of patients monitored during treatment did not show any worsening. Overall, there were no patient dropouts due to adverse events.
sections.discussion:
With recent advances in targeted therapies, patients with psoriasis desire faster and more sustained responses. In our effort to provide dramatic treatment outcomes, our experience with ixekizumab has been extremely positive and encouraging. All 40 patients in our study showed improvement in PASI and BSA at 2, 4, and 12-week follow-up visits.

Absolute PASI and BSA values were extremely relevant in this study for monitoring response. The mean and median absolute values at the end of 12 weeks were less than 5 for PASI, BSA, and DLQI, and the response was statistically significant ( P < 0.001). Similar results were reported by Seidl et al .,[] who found that 72.5% of patients achieved an absolute PASI ≤5 (55.0% ≤3; 42.5% ≤2) at the end of 12 weeks. Mrowietz et al ., also reported that PASI <1, <2, <3, and <5 were achieved by 71.3%, 80.1%, 85.6%, and 88.1% of patients, respectively.[]

Four (10%) patients achieved PASI 75 at the end of 2 weeks, demonstrating a rapid onset of treatment effects, as also highlighted by Blauvelt et al .,[] where at week 2, patients on ixekizumab had a 16-fold greater relative PASI improvement compared to guselkumab. However, our PASI 75 response at 2 weeks was lower than in the referenced study, where 23% (119/520) of patients achieved PASI 75 at 2 weeks. At 4 weeks, PASI 90 was achieved by eight (20%) patients. Similar results were reported by Blauvelt et al .,[] where a PASI 90 response was achieved by 21% (109/520) of patients at 4 weeks with ixekizumab. None of our patients achieved PASI 100 at 4 weeks. PASI 75/90/100 responses at the end of the induction phase (12 weeks) were 100%, 80%, and 20%, respectively, which were similar to the responses reported by Demirel Öğüt et al .[] (92.4%, 86.1%, and 26.6%) at week 16.

The mean and the median values at 12 weeks of treatment were less than five for both biologic naïve and biologic experienced patients []. This finding highlights that all 11 patients who had primary or secondary failure to a previous biologic (TNFi or IL17i) showed a comparable response to ixekizumab, similar to that achieved by biologic naïve patients. Lebwohl et al .[] concluded in their study that switching biologic classes to ixekizumab led to improvements in BSA, DLQI, skin itch, and pain. Our patients also had significant improvement in itch and an overall improvement in DLQI.

Regarding side effects, Blauvelt et al . reported that a small subset of patients experienced upper respiratory tract infections and injection site reactions.[] In our study, a few patients experienced mild-to-moderate itching within 24 hours after the first 160 mg dose. No other side effects were observed.

The study had a small sample size and covered only the induction phase of treatment, resulting in a short follow-up period. Thus, this study lacks the promulgation of long-term treatment outcomes. Commenting on long-term adverse events of ixekizumab is also not possible based on results of this study. Difficult-to-treat sites and high-impact sites, such as the scalp, palms and soles, genitals, and face, were not separately studied. Our study did not include a treatment cost analysis or a comparison with the costs of other available biologics and small molecules.

Ixekizumab is a newer biologic option for the treatment of plaque psoriasis. The study offers significant evidence regarding faster and sustained PASI and BSA response with minimal to no side effects in the Indian population. Ixekizumab offers an equivalent response in biologic naïve patients and in those who had primary or secondary failure to either secukinumab or TNFi inhibitors. Concomitant use of methotrexate is not necessitated, as most patients achieved PASI 90 and both median and mean absolute PASI of <5 at the end of 12 weeks of treatment. This pilot study gives us confidence to use the molecule for a larger population and longer duration.

We confirm that all authors have read and approved the manuscript for submission. All authors meet authorship criteria, and the manuscript represents honest work.

title: Hypomethylation of HLA-DRB1 and its clinical significance in psoriasis.
abstract: Increasing evidences indicate that the abnormal DNA methylation is involved in the pathogenesis of psoriasis. A number of SNPs in HLA-DRB1 have been found being associated with the risk of psoriasis, however it is unclear that metylation status within HLA-DRB1 in psoriasis. Here, DNA and RNA were obtained from epidermis of 56 patients with plaque psoriasis and 28 healthy volunteers served as the control group. For the first time, we discovered mean methylation rate for HLA-DRB1 is 52.2%, 64.3% and 68.1% in epidermis from psoriatic lesions, psoriatic non-lesions and healthy controls, respectively. HLA-DRB1 methylation in psoriatic lesions is significantly lower than in psoriatic non-lesions (t = 13.077, p < 0.001). However, there is no significant difference for HLA-DRB1 methylation between in psoriatic non-lesions and in healthy controls (t = 1.046, p = 0.299). HLA-DRB1 methylation in psoriatic lesions is negatively correlated to PASI score (r = -0.431, p = 0.001). HLA-DRB1 methylation in psoriatic lesions of the patients with onset age≤18 years is significantly lower than the other patients (t = 3.968, p < 0.001). Meanwhile, HLA-DRB1 mRNA expression is significantly increased in psoriatic lesions comparing to psoriatic non-lesions (t = 12.119, p < 0.001). There are no significant difference for HLA-DRB1 mRNA expression between in psoriatic non-lesions and in healthy controls (t = 1.172, p = 0,245). Moreover, HLA-DRB1 mRNA expression is negatively associated with HLA-DRB1 methylation in psoriatic lesions (r = 0.932, p < 0.001). In conclusions, our results showed hypomethylation of HLA-DRB1 is associated with HLA-DRB1 mRNA expression and severity of the disease, indicating that hypomethylation of HLA-DRB1 may play roles in the pathogenesis of psoriasis.

sections.other:
Psoriasis is a common chronic skin disorder that affected about 1%-3% of the world population, and the pathogenesis of psoriasis is still unclear. Based on current findings, psoriasis is generally considered as an autoimmune disease caused by T cell-mediated hyperproliferation of the keratinocytes []. Increasing evidences indicate that psoriasis is also a genetic disease triggered by multiple environmental factors, such as smoking, chronic infections, stress, climate changes. Many studies about the association between human leukocyte antigens (HLA) and psoriasis have been reported for a long time [, ]. In recent studies, much attention have been paid on the role of epigenetic changes (e.g. DNA methylation) in psoriasis, and the abnormal epigenetic modification of several molecules has been observed in the psoriatic lesions of patients [, ]; however, researchers still need to make greater efforts to illustrate the mechanism of how the aberrant epigenetic modifications would affect the pathogenesis of psoriasis.

Human leukocyte antigen class (HLA)-DRB1 is a transmembrane heterodimer cell surface receptor with α and β chains, and each contains extracellular domains, membrane-spanning domain and a tail anchored in the cytoplasm. The α chain of HLA-DRB1 lack polymorphism, and the β chain is encoded by 4 loci DRB1, DRB3, DRB4 and DRB5 []. HLA-DRB1 is a major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class II protein that expressed constitutively by antigen-presenting cells (APCs), such as dendritic cells, macrophages etc. The expression of HLA-DRB1 is important for APCs, because HLA-DRB1 can determine the efficiency of APCs to present antigen to T cells [].

Several studies have examined the relationship between HLA-DRB1 and cancer, including parotid cancer [] and ovarian cancer []. Previous studies suggested that immunohistochemically detectable HLA-DRB1 expression is associated with better prognosis in patients with colorectal cancer [, , ]. The relationship between HLA-DRB1 and AIDs has also been reported. The level of expression of HLA-DRB1 alleles have been associated with the development of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), rheumatoid arthritis (RA), systemic sclerosis (SSc) and multiple sclerosis (MS) [].

Although the HLA class II locus is the strong genetic risk factor for RA, the relationship between HLA class II alleles and lymphocyte activation remains unclear. The presence of HLA-DR was not confined to activated CD4+ and CD8+ T cells []. Nagafuchi et al. [] studied immunophenotyping of peripheral blood mononuclear cells on RA patients with HLA-DRB1genotype and found the frequency of memory CXCR4+CD4+ T cells was significantly related to severity of disease. A significantly higher frequency of memory CXCR4+CD4+ T cells was found in the patients with one or more susceptible HLA-DR haplotypes, moreover, on B cells, the frequency of memory CXCR4+CD4+ T cells significantly was associated with the HLA-DR expression, which suggested that the interaction between HLA-DR and T cell receptors can regulate the memory CXCR4+CD4+ T cells.

In psoriasis, the role of HLA-DRB1 has also been well investigated. As early as 1982, VB Morhenn et al first observed the abnormal expression of HLA-DRB1 in skin samples of patients with psoriasis []. Since then, the polymorphism of HLA-DRB1 and its relationship with the psoriasis, as well as the role of HLA-DRB1 alleles in the pathogensis of psoriasis have been reported in different works [, , , ]. The functional role of the HLA-DRB1 molecule in psoriasis remains enigmatic. In psoriasis, Keratin 17 is a major target antigen of autoreactive T cells. On Keratin 17, the epitopes S1 (118-132), S2 (169-183), S4 (323-337) and S4 (348-362) of HLA-DRB1*04, *07-restricted T cell epitope regions are immunodominant HLA-DRB1-restricted T cell epitopes []. Magalhães et al [] demonstrate these polymorphisms of HLA class I and II may be genetic risk for severity of the disease in a case-control study of patients with mild or severe psoriasis, and found that alleles HLA-DRB1*07, B*37, Cw*06 and Cw*12 were correlated with severe disease course.

However, to our knowledge, the methylation status of HLA-DRB1 in psoratic patients has not yet been investigated. In our previous work, we already proved that hypermethylation of HLA-C may play an important role in psoriasis []. In this study, we will focus on the methylation status of HLA-DRB1 in psoriasis and its relationship with the disease.
sections.results:
First, we performed bisulfite sequencing PCR (BSP) analysis to determine the methylation status in the promoter regions of HLA-DRB1 in epidermis of psoriatic lesions, psoriatic non-lesions and healthy volunteers. Methylation of HLA-DRB1 was found in all samples, and bisulfite sequencing results indicated that 3-18 of 18 CpG dinucleotides in the promoter region of the HLA-DRB1 were methylated (Figure and ). In psoriatic lesions, psoriatic non-lesions and healthy controls, the mean rate of promoter methylation for HLA-DRB1 was 52.26±2.66%, 64.34±2.30% and 68.11±2.18%, respectively. The frequency of promoter methylation for HLA-DRB1 in psoriatic lesions was significantly lower than in psoriatic non-lesions ( t = 13.077, p < 0.001), and there is no significant difference for the rate of HLA-DRB1 methylation between in psoriatic non-lesions and healthy controls ( t = 1.046, p = 0.299) (Figure ). The mean methylation rate of HLA-DRB1 of the minors group with onset age≤18 years is significantly lower than the adults group with onset age >18 years in psoriatic lesions (37.43±5.10% and 58.19±2.61%; t = 3.968, p < 0.001) (Figure ). The mean methylation rate of HLA-DRB1 in psoriatic lesions is negatively correlated to PASI score ( r = -0.431, p = 0.001) (Figure ).

In order to examine whether HLA-DRB1 methylation can affect the level of HLA-DRB1 expression in psoriasis, we performed RT-PCR analysis to determine the level of HLA-DRB1 mRNA in the specimens of epidermis. We have observed the expression of HLA-DRB1 in 94.6% (53/56) psoriatic lesions, 92.9% (52/58) psoriatic non-lesions and 92.9% (26/28) epidermis of healthy controls. The mean mRNA expression of HLA-DRB1 in psoriatic lesions, psoriatic non-lesions and healthy controls is 0.57±0.03, 0.47±0.03 and 0.41±0.03, respectively (Figure ). HLA-DRB1 mRNA expression in psoriatic lesions was higher than psoriatic non-lesions ( t = 12.119, p < 0.001). There are no significant difference for the expression of HLA-DRB1 mRNA between in psoriatic non-lesions and healthy controls ( t = 1.172, p = 0.245). The mean value of HLA-DRB1 mRNA expression is negatively correlated to the methylation of HLA-DRB1 in psoriatic lesions( r = -0.932, p < 0.001) (Figure ).
sections.discussion:
DNA methylation is an important epigenetic mechanism that can affect gene expression without changing the DNA sequence. Some recent studies indicated that aberrant methylation status of HLA genes may be involved in the pathogenesis of some diseases. The abnormal methylation of HLA-G gene has been found in cancers [, ] and preeclampsia []; and hypermethylation of HLA-A, B, C was observed in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) []. For HLA-DRB1, Hu et al. proved that HLA-DRB1B1 methylation changes can promote the occurrence and progression of ESCC []; Yu et al. reported the association between brain DNA methylation of HLA-DRB1B5 and pathological diagnosis of Alzheimer disease []; Graves et al. discovered that methylation at the HLA-DRB1B1 locus in CD4+ T cells are associated with multiple sclerosis [].

In our study, we first reported the hypomethylation of HLA-DRB1 in psoriatic epidermis; more importantly, our data proved that methylation of HLA-DRB1 is negatively correlated with the severity of the disease, suggesting that the methylation status of HLA-DRB1 can become a potential bio-marker for the diagnosis or evaluating the efficacy of treatment of psoriasis. Interestingly, previous work has also correlated aberrant methylation of HLA-DRB1 with the prognosis of some diseases, thus, we hypothesis that methylation status of HLA-DRB1 may also affect the prognosis and recurrence of psoriasis, which can be proposed as our future direction for the investigation of HLA-DRB1 methylation in psoriasis.

Roberson et al. [] found that the frequency of methylation was strongly associated with gene expression at a nearby locus at only 12/1,100 CpG sites, suggesting that the level of methylation may only affect the expression of a small size of genes. The promoter and 3’-UTR of HLA-DRB1 can antagonistically regulate the gene expression []. In order to explore if HLA-DRB1 promoter hypomethylation can directly affect the expression of HLA-DRB1, we also examined HLA-DRB1 mRNA expression in all epidermis from psoriatic lesions, psoriatic non-lesions and healthy controls. The expression of HLA-DRB1 mRNA was significantly increased in psoriatic epidermis when compared with the healthy volunteers, and the mean value of HLA-DRB1 mRNA expression is negatively correlated to the promoter methylation of HLA-DRB1. Our results indicated that hypomethylation of HLA-DRB1 may be one of the leading causes that induced the overexpression of HLA-DRB1 in psoriatic epidermis, which may promote the development of the disease.

The impact of the hypomethylation and overexpression of HLA-DRB1 on keratinocytes is still unclear. It was demonstrated that several peptides on keratin 17 can serve as immunodominant T-cell epitopes and stimulate peripheral blood lymphocytes of HLA DRB1*04 and/or *07 positive patients with psoriasis. Moreover, the peptide ligands are able to inhibit proliferation of T cells and keratinocyte in psoriasis [].

One limitation of present study is that we only performed analysis of HLA-DRB1 expression on mRNA level for the limited epidermal specimens, and the expression of HLA-DRB1 protein in samples have not been examined. For every patient, only a small piece of epidermis could be collected, thus the samples were not enough for both nucleic acid level and protein level analysis. To investigate the specific role of hypomethylation of HLA-DRB1 in the pathogenesis of psoriasis, in the following step, we plan to perform animal studies using the existing psoratic models.

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first paper reporting an association between methylation of HLA-DRB1 gene and psoriasis. Overall, abnormal hypomethylation of HLA-DRB1 gene promoter has been observed in psoriatic epidermis. Hypomethylation of HLA-DRB1 associated with the mRNA level of HLA-DRB1 expression and severity of the disease, indicating that hypomethylation of HLA-DRB1 may also play a potential role in the pathogenesis of psoriasis.
sections.methods:
Skin samples were collected from 56 patients with active plaque psoriasis (21 females and 35 males) and 28 healthy volunteers. Their characteristics are summarized in Table . A paired psoriatic lesion (PP) and psoriatic non-lesion (PN) were derived from the same patient, thus a total number of 56 paired PP/PN samples were obtained. The psoriatic non-lesion specimens were taken from the sites more than 5 cm far away lesion edge. The patients were between 18 to 65 years old (mean 37.25±1.68), with the length of disease ranged from 1 to 33 years (mean 7.41±0.99). Among all 56 patients, the onset age of 40 cases was more than 18 years old. The severity of the disease was evaluated using the psoriasis area severity index (PASI) scoring system and the score was ranged from 4 to 46 (mean 16.78±1.27). Patients that received either systemic or topical therapy 6 weeks prior to this study and pregnant patients were excluded. Healthy volunteers (NN) were people who did not have skin lesions and without self-reported psoriasis history. The NN group and PP/PN group has a qualified match in age and sex. All tissue specimens were obtained following the ethical guidelines mandated by the ethical committee of Institute of Dermatology, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences who approved this study. All candidates were approached using approved ethical guidelines and those who agreed to participate in this study were required to sign the consent forms. Tissue specimens on trunk or limbs were obtained using a 6-mm punch biopsy under aseptic conditions with local anesthesia. The specimens were frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C until processed.

Epidermis were separated from skin specimens using 0.25% Dispase (Roche, USA) for 6-12 hours; next, the samples were placed on ice, and homogenized in sterilized 5-mL tissue grinders; then, DNA and total RNA were extracted from the epidermis samples using QIAamp DNA Mini kit and RNA Mini kit (Qiagen, Valentia, CA) following the manufacturer's protocols. The quality of the extracted total RNA were assessed using electrophoresis on 1% agarose gels, by visualizing the 18S and 28S RNA bands under UV light.

Bisulphite conversion of genomic DNA was performed was performed using EpiTectH Bisulfite kit (Qiagen) following the manufacturer's instructions. Briefly, genomic DNA samples (50 ~ 150 ng DNA/sample) were denatured using NaOH, and then treated with sodium bisulfite; next, the samples were desulfonated,and purified using silica-membrane columns; finally, the treated DNAs were suspended in 10μl TE buffer either for immediate measurement, or stored at -20 °C for future analysis.

To investigate the methylation status of the HLA-DRB1 promoter, we mapped the corresponding CpG island in HLA-DRB1 by CpGplot (EBI Tools, EMBOSS CpGPlot; http://www.ebi.ac.uk/emboss/cpgplot ). CpG-enriched region of HLA-DRB1 was amplified using primers as follow: F-5’- TTTTAGGTAGATGGAAGAGGAA -3’ and R-5’- AACAACCCAAAAAATTCTTCTA -3’ (352bp). Modified DNAs were used for PCR analysis, and the products include 18 CpG sites and span part of the promoter of HLA-DRB1. The reaction was set up at a total volume of 25 ml containing 1 ml sample DNA, 0.2 mM dNTPs, 0.5 mM primers, 2.5 mM MgCl2, 16buffer II, and 1.25 unit HotTaq DNA polymerase (Takara, JP).The thermocycle profiles was 94 °C for 9 minutes to activate the polymerase; 44 cycles at 94 °C for 30 seconds, 55 °C for 30 seconds, and 68 °C for 45 seconds; and a 7-minute terminal extension at 68 °C. The amplified DNA fragments were then cloned into plasmids using a TOPO TA Cloning kit (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA) according to manufacturer's instructions .The clones were then screened by colony PCR, and purified using the Qiaquick kit (Qiagen, CA). Next, individual clones were sequenced on an ABI PRISM 3730 automated sequencer, and the sequence electropherograms were aligned using Sequence Navigator software (Applied Biosystems). Quantitative methylation rates were estimated from sequence traces using the ESME software.

Total RNA extracted from epidermis was converted to amplified cDNA using a GoScript™ Reverse Tanscription System Kit (Promega, USA) on the DNA Engine Opticon System (ABI GeneAmp PCR System 7300, USA), and cDNAs were aliquoted and stored at -20 °C. In brief, the cDNA synthesis contained 5 uL of 10× Taqman RT buffer; 11 uL of 25 mM MgCl2; 10 uL of deoxy NTPs; 2.5 uL of Oligo d(T)16 primer; 1 uL of RNase inhibitor; 1.25uL of Multiscribe reverse transcriptase, and 1 ug of RNA. Two separate 50 uL reactions for each RNA were performed and combined together. Each cDNA batch reaction had a maximum of 24 tubes to ensure the best sample quality. Primers were as follow: HLA-DRB1 F- 5’- TGCCAAGTGGAGCACCCAA -3’ and R-5’- GCATCTTGCTCTGTGCAGAT -3’; β-ACTIN F-5’- CAGTCGGTTGGAGCGAGCAT -3’ and R-5’- GGACTTCCTGTAACAACGCATCT -3’. The primer test results showed that all cDNA amplified with a single band. This detection ensured that the primers were specific to HLA-DRB1. Quantitative PCR (qPCR) was performed on an ABI 7900HT Sequence Detection System (Applied Biosystems) in 384-well plates. The samples were run in triplicate using one plate per gene. The reaction was performed in a 12.5 uL total volume with 6.5 uL of 2× SYBR Green Master Mix (Applied Biosystems); 0.25 uL of 10 uM forward primer; 0.25 uL of 10 uM reverse primer; 4uL of a 1:10 dilution of cDNA template (corresponding to approximately 8 ng RNA). The thermal cycle conditions were: 50 °C for 2 min, 95 °C for 10 min, 45 cycles at 95 °C for 15 s, and 62 °C for 1 min, and a final dissociation step at 95 °C for 15 s, 65 °C for 15 s, and 95 °C for 15 s. The qPCR cycle threshold (Ct) was set in the middle of the exponential phase of the amplification. Also, appropriate positive and negative controls were included in each run. In each experiment, the individual sample was run in triplicate and the Ct of each well was recorded at the end of the reaction. The mean and standard deviation (SD) of the three Cts were calculated and the average value was accepted if the triplicate Ct values were within±1 Ct.

For each sample, HLA-DRB1 expression was presented as the ratio between HLA-DRB1 and the endogenous control (β-ACTIN) using the 2−ΔΔCt method []. The identity of polymerase chain reaction (PCR) products was verified by sequencing.

SPSS 17.0 was used for all statistic analyses. The methylation and RT-PCR results are presented as mean ± SE. The t-test was used to compare the difference between paired and unpaired observations. Adjusted odds ratios (ORs) were calculated by fitting logistic regression models with adjustment. P -values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant.

title: Histologic comparison of tumor necrosis factor-α inhibitor-induced psoriasis and psoriasis vulgaris.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Tumor necrosis factor-α inhibitor (TNFi)-induced psoriasis is a paradoxic reaction characterized by the development of a psoriasiform rash that mimics idiopathic psoriasis subtypes both clinically and histologically. Few studies have investigated the histologic features of TNFi-induced psoriasis skin lesions, and most of these are limited by inclusion of few specimens. OBJECTIVE: We aimed to characterize histologic features of TNFi-induced psoriasis and identify histologic differences between TNFi-induced psoriasis and idiopathic psoriasis. METHODS: We characterized 60 biopsy specimens obtained from 47 unique patients at a single tertiary care referral center between 2004 and 2016 who developed TNFi-induced psoriasis, and we compared histologic features to those of 85 biopsy specimens from a control group of 85 patients with idiopathic psoriasis. RESULTS: The most common histologic reaction pattern in TNFi-induced psoriasis biopsy specimens was psoriasiform (80.0%). Five histologic parameters were significantly different in TNFi-induced psoriasis biopsy specimens compared with idiopathic psoriasis biopsy specimens: at least 3 dermal eosinophils per histologic section, neutrophils in the stratum corneum, neutrophils in the epidermis, papillary plate thinning, and absence of parakeratosis. LIMITATIONS: Inability to exclude lesion selection bias as a potential reason for some significant histologic differences. CONCLUSIONS: This study supports the idea that histologic differences exist between TNFi-induced psoriasis and idiopathic psoriasis may help distinguish between these conditions, especially for dermal eosinophil counts of 3 or greater.

title: Pharmacological inhibition of TXNRD1 attenuates psoriasis-like dermatitis by suppressing keratinocyte proliferation and NF-κB signaling.
abstract: Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease characterized by excessive keratinocyte proliferation and immune activation. Thioredoxin reductase 1 (TXNRD1), a key enzyme of the thioredoxin antioxidant system, regulates cellular redox balance and inflammatory signaling; however, its functional role in psoriasis remains unclear. Here, we demonstrate that TXNRD1 expression is markedly upregulated in lesional skin from psoriasis patients and in imiquimod-induced psoriasis-like dermatitis in mice. Genetic deletion of TXNRD1 in keratinocytes significantly suppressed cell proliferation, reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine production, and diminished chemotactic activity toward CD4+ T cells in vitro. Importantly, topical administration of the TXNRD1 inhibitor TRi markedly alleviated psoriasis-like skin inflammation in vivo, as evidenced by reduced epidermal hyperplasia and decreased CD4+ T cell infiltration. Mechanistically, TNF-α and IFN-γ induced TXNRD1 expression and activated NF-κB signaling in keratinocytes. TXNRD1 deficiency significantly attenuated TNF-α/IFN-γ-induced NF-κB phosphorylation, leading to reduced chemokine expression and impaired T-cell recruitment. These findings identify TXNRD1 as a critical regulator of keratinocyte-driven inflammatory responses and provide pharmacological evidence supporting TXNRD1 as a potential therapeutic target for psoriasis.

title: Efficacy and safety of various drug combinations in treating plaque Psoriasis: A meta-analysis
abstract: Background Psoriasis, a chronic inflammatory disease affecting the skin, joints, and nails (2-3% worldwide), significantly affects quality of life. Genetic and environmental factors also play key roles. Topical corticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors, and oral corticosteroids help to manage plaque psoriasis symptoms, but combination therapies might offer greater effectiveness and improved safety profiles. These combinations could potentially reduce medication dosages and side effects in patients. Objective To assess the efficacy and safety of various drug combinations over conventional monotherapies in the treatment of moderate to severe plaque psoriasis, which incorporates palmoplantar psoriasis and psoriasis vulgaris, by discovering and utilizing research articles comprising the same or similar variables as PASI 75 and evaluating the information using RevMan v5.4.1. Method We reviewed the efficacy and safety of combination therapy vs. monotherapy/placebo for moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis (palmoplantar and vulgaris) using PASI 75 via RevMan v5.4.1. Risk of bias assessment and funnel plots were employed to assess the heterogeneity of each paper. Inclusion criteria – Publications 20 yrs. Results Seventeen studies were analyzed, comprising a total of 2291 patients (n=1147 with combination regimens and n=1144 with control regimen in the analysis). A significant PASI 75- response was observed in the pioglitazone combination subgroup as compared to placebo (OR=4.92,95% CI 2.19-11.05, P = 0.0001); methotrexate combination subgroup as compared to placebo (OR=2.56, 95% CI 1.67-3.94, P< 0.0001) test of subgroup differences showed P= 0.14, I 2 = 34%. title: Integrated Mechanism Study of Rehmanniae Radix–Sophorae Flos for Psoriasis Treatment Based on UPLC-Q-TOF/MS, Network Pharmacology, Mendelian Randomization, and Molecular Docking
abstract: Background: and Objectives: To elucidate the material basis and molecular mechanisms of the Rehmanniae Radix–Sophorae Flos (RR-SF) herb pair for psoriasis treatment, and to verify causal effects of core targets from a genetic perspective, constructing an integrated “component–target–pathway–causality” evidence chain. Materials and Methods: A four-level strategy was employed: (1) UPLC-Q-TOF/MS identified chemical constituents of the RR-SF co-decoction; (2) network pharmacology screened active compounds (OB ≥ 30%, DL ≥ 0.10), predicted targets, constructed drug–compound–target–pathway and PPI networks, and performed GO/KEGG enrichment; (3) drug-target Mendelian randomization (MR) used eQTLs of 7 core targets as exposure and psoriasis GWAS as outcome, with IVW as primary method and MR-Egger, Cochran’s Q, leave-one-out, and Steiger tests for sensitivity analysis; (4) AutoDock Vina molecular docking verified binding between active compounds and core targets. Results: 109 constituents were identified, dominated by flavonoids (32), iridoids (26), and phenylethanoid glycosides (12). Network pharmacology yielded 14 active compounds and 159 shared targets, with SRC, MAPK3, RXRA, HSP90AA1, CTNNB1, AKT1, and MAPK1 as core hubs. Key pathways included IL-17, MAPK, Th17 differentiation, VEGF, PI3K-Akt, and NF-κB. MR confirmed causal associations: MAPK1 (OR = 2.58, 95% CI 1.49–4.46, P = 7.5 × 10⁻⁴, risk), HSP90AA1 (OR = 0.42, 95% CI 0.24–0.74, P = 2.6 × 10⁻³, protective), and SRC (OR = 2.00, 95% CI 1.04–3.87, P = 0.039). MAPK1 and HSP90AA1 remained significant after Bonferroni correction. Molecular docking identified quercetin–HSP90AA1 (−9.3 kcal/mol) and aeginetic acid–RXRA (−9.1 kcal/mol) as strongest interactions. Conclusions: RR-SF exerts anti-psoriatic effects via a multi-component–multi-target–multi-pathway mode. MR validated causality of core targets, and molecular docking identified quercetin–HSP90AA1 and aeginetic acid–RXRA as key intervention strategies, providing multi-dimensional evidence for precision psoriasis treatment.

title: Phenotype Switching in Pediatric Inflammatory Skin Diseases During Biologic Therapy: A Literature Review Focused on Atopic Dermatitis and Psoriasis
abstract: Biologic therapies are highly efficacious for pediatric atopic dermatitis (AD) and psori-asis (PsO); however, their expanding use has led to increased reports of phenotype switching—a paradoxical condition where biologics induce new-onset im-mune-mediated dermatoses. To address clinical uncertainty regarding these complex reactions, this review evaluates real-world case reports, case series, and observational studies of pediatric AD and PsO patients who developed phenotypic switching during biologic therapy. Dupilumab is the most frequently implicated agent, commonly in-ducing psoriasiform, pustular, or palmoplantar eruptions in AD patients via a compen-satory shift from Th2- to Th17-predominant immunity. Conversely, phenotype switch-ing from IL-12/23 and TNF-α inhibitors remains rare in pediatric dermatology. For se-vere, refractory cases or AD-PsO overlaps, Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors demonstrate significant rescue efficacy, provided appropriate baseline and ongoing laboratory mon-itoring is maintained. Pediatric patients experiencing biologic-induced phenotype switching can be successfully managed in clinical practice through early recognition and the implementation of the practical, evidence-based treatment algorithm proposed in this review.

title: Psoriasis-like skin inflammation drives an elongated mitochondrial network marked by functional failure in keratinocytes.
abstract: BackgroundPsoriasis is characterized by a pathogenic, hyperproliferative state of keratinocytes. While inflammation is known to drive this proliferation and induce metabolic reprogramming to regulate immune effector functions, the specific mitochondrial and metabolic alterations in keratinocytes during psoriatic inflammation remain poorly understood.ObjectiveTo determine how cutaneous inflammation dynamically modulates mitochondrial networks and bioenergetics within the epidermal compartment, and to evaluate the metabolic consequences of disrupting this morphology.MethodsUsing a standardized mouse model of psoriasis-like inflammation, keratinocyte culture and in silico human psoriatic samples, we assessed mitochondrial health. We analyzed mitochondrial membrane potential and quantified metabolites associated with the Tricarboxylic Acid (TCA) cycle. Additionally, we evaluated the expression and activity of mitochondrial fusion and structural synthesis machinery in mouse tissues.ResultsImiquimod-driven inflammation induces mitochondrial dysfunction, marked by reduced membrane potential and suppression of key TCA cycle intermediates. Rather than undergoing fragmentation, psoriatic keratinocytes exhibit a shift toward fused network state marked by Pgc-1α presence. Pharmacological disruption of this architecture via Mdivi-1 fails to restore function and ameliorate disease progression in vivo; instead, it increases reactive oxygen species production and acts synergistically with IL-17A to robustly amplify pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion.ConclusionThis study shows that an elongated, fused mitochondrial network architecture is a feature of the epidermal compartment under chronic psoriatic inflammation. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that promoting this structural state via mitochondrial division inhibitors does not improve psoriasis-like inflammation in vivo but rather exacerbates cellular oxidative stress and sustains skin inflammation.

title: Keratinocyte-specific STAT3 knockout attenuates imiquimod-induced psoriasiform phenotype in mice.
abstract: Signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) is critical in psoriasis, but keratinocyte-derived STAT3 remains unclear. This study investigated the effect of keratinocyte-specific STAT3 knockout on imiquimod (IMQ)-induced psoriasis-like dermatitis. Keratinocyte-specific STAT3 knockout (cKO) mice and littermate controls (LC) received daily topical 5% IMQ to induce psoriasis-like lesions. Lesion severity was assessed by PASI score, histopathology by H&E staining, and systemic inflammation by spleen index and serum CXCL1, CCL20, and IL-22 levels (ELISA). Skin expression of inflammation, chemokine, and STAT3 pathway related factors was examined by IHC, qRT-PCR, and Western blot. In vitro, IL-17A‑stimulated HaCaT cells were used with siRNA-mediated STAT3 knockdown; changes in STAT3 signaling and downstream factors were assessed by qRT-PCR and Western blot. In vivo, keratinocyte-specific STAT3 knockout significantly alleviated IMQ-induced skin lesions, reduced PASI score, improved barrier function, decreased spleen index, and lowered serum CXCL1, CCL20, and IL-22. It also suppressed IL-22, CXCL1, and CCL20 expression in skin and inhibited STAT3 activation. In vitro, IL-17A increased STAT3 phosphorylation, which was blocked by STAT3 knockdown, along with suppression of IL-22 and CXCL1 upregulation.

title: Comparative Transcriptomics Reveals SKH-1 Mice as a Valuable Model for Psoriasis Pathogenesis and Recurrence Studies.
abstract: Psoriasis is a complex chronic inflammatory and autoimmune disease; therefore, reliable and human-relevant animal models are essential for preclinical drug testing and mechanistic studies. SKH-1 mice, which lack functional hair follicles and display a thickened epidermis that more closely resembles human skin than that of C57BL/6 mice, represent a potential psoriasis model, but their suitability remains uncertain. In this study, proliferation, barrier function, differentiation, and inflammatory responses were assessed in the imiquimod (IMQ)-induced dermatitis model of SKH-1 mice using qRT-PCR, immunofluorescence, and flow cytometry. Transcriptomic profiling via RNA sequencing was performed on total RNA from lesional and non-lesional skin of IMQ-induced SKH-1 mice, IMQ-induced C57BL/6 mice, and human psoriatic skin. A psoriasis-like mouse model was also established in SKH-1 mice to evaluate its utility for recurrence studies. The results showed that the IMQ-induced SKH-1 mouse model exhibited hyperproliferation, hypodifferentiation, barrier disruption, and excessive inflammatory responses similar to human psoriasis. Transcriptomic analysis further highlighted the advantages and complementarity of this model in studying psoriasis pathogenesis, and the established recurrence model provided a suitable tool for investigating the mechanisms of psoriasis recurrence. This study compared the transcriptomic signatures of lesional skin between IMQ-induced SKH-1 and C57BL/6 mice and demonstrated that the SKH-1 model can recapitulate vascular dysregulation and disease recurrence, indicating that it serves as a valuable complementary tool for probing psoriasis pathogenesis.

title: Clinical predictors of psoriatic arthritis and osteoclast differentiation.
abstract: Psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis (PsA) are interrelated inflammatory diseases. Psoriasis usually precedes PsA onset and represents a well-established risk factor for PsA development. Bone erosion is a hallmark of PsA, and the contribution of cutaneous psoriatic inflammation in this process has been demonstrated. However, little is still known on the pathogenetic mechanisms that link psoriatic skin to joint damage. Clinical features of psoriatic disease, including specific body site involvement, seem to be important risk predictors of PsA. The aim of this pilot research study was to investigate if psoriatic cutaneous inflammation, affecting these anatomical predictive sites for PsA, could be linked to osteoclast differentiation and activity. Our results showed that psoriasis skin localizations were positively related to the osteoclastogenic profile in psoriatic patients. These results provide new insights into the fascinating skin-joint axis concept.

title: Myeloid PGGT1B Deficiency Promotes Psoriasiform Dermatitis by Promoting the Secretion of Inflammatory Factors.
abstract: Psoriasis pathogenesis involves dysregulated immune responses, yet the role of protein prenylation (particularly PGGT1B-mediated geranylgeranylation) in macrophage-driven inflammation remains poorly understood. This study aims to explore the role and molecular mechanism of protein geranylgeranyltransferase type I subunit beta (PGGT1B) in the development of psoriasis. Myeloid cell-specific PGGT1B gene knockout mice were generated, and a mouse psoriasis model was established with imiquimod to study the role and mechanism of PGGT1B gene downregulation-induced macrophage activation in the pathogenesis of psoriasis. Bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs) from wild-type and PGGT1B knockout mice were cultured and stimulated with resiquimod (R848) to simulate the immune microenvironment of psoriasis. In addition, the differentially expressed genes induced by PGGT1B knockout were analyzed using RNA-seq, and bioinformatics analysis was carried out to study the possible biological process of PGGT1B regulation. Finally, PMA-THP-1 was co-cultured with HaCaT cells to study the effect of PGGT1B deletion in macrophages on the proliferation and differentiation of keratinocytes. Bone marrow PGGT1B deficiency aggravated the psoriasis-like lesions induced by imiquimod in mice. In BMDMs with PGGT1B deficiency, the NF-κB signaling pathway was over-activated by R848, and the expressions of proinflammatory cytokines IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α were significantly increased. Activation of cell division cycle 42 (CDC42) may mediate the activation of the NF-κB pathway in PGGT1B-deficient BMDMs. PGGT1B deletion can promote the proliferation and inhibit the differentiation of HaCaT cells. Reduced PGGT1B levels can increase the expression of CDC42, which further activates NLRP3 inflammation in macrophages through NF-κB signaling, further aggravating the inflammatory state of psoriasis. Psoriasis-like lesions induced by IMQ are aggravated when PGGT1B expression is reduced in mouse bone marrow cells. A possible mechanism for this is that PGGT1B-deficient macrophages migrate to the epidermis more easily during psoriasis, which leads to the activation of Cdc42, NF-κB signaling, and NLRP3 inflammatory corpuscles.
