sections.results:
It has been well demonstrated that Mg presents as a promising next-generation biodegradable metal of excellent biocompatibility, which offers high capacity of hydrogen storage with thermal stability, particularly in small size []. Herein, high-purity, submicron-scale magnesium hydride particles (MgH 2 , denoted as HydroMg) were synthesized using the arc plasma evaporation method as we previously reported []. Transmission electron microscope (TEM) images of nano-MgH 2 revealed a spheroidal, polyhedron morphology, with an average size of ∼280 nm (B and C). The crystal structure of as-prepared MgH 2 was confirmed with XRD, as the characteristic peaks were consistent with the standard (JCPDS card no. 12-0697, D). Mg powders had almost completely transformed into MgH 2 hydride upon hydrogenation, barely leaving unreacted Mg or oxidized MgO. The thermal stability behavior of MgH 2 were characterized by TGA/DSC (). Meanwhile, the resultant powder was characterized with ca. 7.1 wt% hydrogen absorption at 450 °C, quite close to the maximum theoretical value of 7.6 wt%, which verified with an outstanding loading content of hydrogen. Of note, such a gas-phase synthesis approach could be scaled up to mass production of high-quality MgH 2 with controllable nanoscale size. To ensure long-term stability and batch-to-batch consistency, the MgH 2 nanoparticles are maintained in a dry, vacuum-sealed environment at room temperature prior to use.

Subsequently, to deliver the as-synthesized hydrogen-storage MgH 2 particles to psoriasis lesions for continuous generation of H 2 , a thermosensitive composite hydrogel with fast gelation was prepared by simply mixing MgH 2 nanoparticles at room temperature in normal saline (0.90% w/v NaCl). For this study, the gelator of polyoxyethylene–polyoxypropylene block copolymer (POE–POP–POE, Pluronic F-127) was prepared, as Pluronics are a class of non-toxic FDA-approved triblock copolymers with amphiphilic nature, which can undergo micellization and gelation with elevated temperature above its LCST (low critical solution temperature). The hydrogel fabrication, hydrogen generation and delivery process of the designated MgH 2 -Gel system was schematically depicted in A, along with the resultant bubble gel displayed in E, revealing a distinct sol-gel phase transition between 22 °C and 35 °C, and exhibiting varied viscosity and thermal sensitivity depending on the various concentrations of the gelator (). The rheological data confirmed that the hydrogel transitioned from a low-viscosity liquid at 4 °C to gel at 25 °C and 35 °C ( and ). The gel (25 wt%) exhibited rapid stabilization, reaching a firm gel state within 20 s at 35 °C. This rapid transition ensured that even if the formulation was applied in a semi-fluid state, it quickly set on the skin, enhancing the localized delivery of H 2 and improving patient compliance. The MgH 2 nanoparticles were then incorporated and uniformly distributed into the gel network through formation of large quantity of hydrogen bonding and ionic bonding with the ether groups in the Pluronic F-127 gelators. MgH 2 -Gel was then obtained through a self-assembly, fast gelling process at skin physiological temperature. From infrared spectra data (), MgH 2 -Gel was a mixture of MgH 2 , and F127 gel, as indicated by their feature peaks at 500-850 cm −1 (Mg‒H vibration of MgH 2 ), 945.97 cm −1 (Mg-OH vibration of Mg(OH) 2 ) and 1083.15 cm −1 (C-O-C vibration of F127). The gel matrix was exploited to play a dual role in this in situ hydrogenation system. In addition to supply aqueous environment for boosting MgH 2 hydrolysis for continuous hydrogen generation, the amphiphilic gelator also subsequently acted as a surfactant to stabilize the produced hydrogen microbubbles, according to the previously proposed skin theory []. Gas bubbles can be effectively covered with organic surfactants forming a skin or shell of the bubbles, which not only lowers the surface tension, but also protects the encapsulated gas from diffusion, thereby allowing for sustained release of hydrogen in this microbubble gel system.

Next, we investigated the effects of microbubble gel properties on gas loading capacities. Microbubble cavities in the as-prepared bubble gel system were immobilized with amphiphilic micelles, which reduced hydrogen bubble breakage and coalescence. Furthermore, a gel network encircling the bubble cavity served as a physical barrier, which slowed down gas diffusion further. The observed microscopic images of freshly-obtained bubbles in gel and its dynamic evolution are shown in , which clearly exhibited abundant microbubbles of nearly uniform distribution with an average diameter of 45 μm, indicating the designated gel system “locked” H 2 gas immediately and immensely. Moreover, even after 4 h and 12 h, the average bubble size only slightly changed to ca. 50 μm and 70 μm, respectively, and a significant number of intact gas microbubbles still retained and embedded in the gel. The presence of the unique H 2 peak in the microbubble-loaded hydrogel (), which provided direct evidence that the gas encapsulated and released by MgH 2 -Gel was indeed hydrogen. In vitro hydrogen-release kinetics of different hydrogen delivery systems were determined by a hydrogen microsensor multimeter. As expected, MgH 2 nanoparticles placed in aqueous solution immediately brought about abundant hydrogen evolution in hydrolysis reaction, but with an undesirable, rapid burst release profile due to its high diffusibility and low solubility in solutions (). In contrast, as observed in G, a significant, continuous release of H 2 from an optimized formulation of MgH 2 -Gel (25 wt/v %) could be well maintained for approximately 2 days, which was significantly prolonged as compared to that in aqueous solution. Moreover, the hydrogen release profile was facilely controlled by tuning the concentration of F-127 gelator, and sustained hydrogen release was obtained from a higher-concentration gelator (25 wt/v %) of adequate rheology to stabilize the self-generated bubbles, which was way more efficient than that of lower-concentration gelators (15 wt/v %). The results shown in H and I were in line with the trend of H 2 release, suggesting the optimized gel formulation also considerably restrained the excessive release of hydrolysis reaction byproducts (Mg 2+ and OH − ), which would be beneficial for improving biosafety and biocompatibility. To further validate this biosafety profile in vivo , we assessed the skin irritation potential of MgH 2 -Gel in mouse models (), alongside histological analysis of major organs (). Moreover, human patch testing on a volunteer confirmed its non-irritating nature and safety for human skin (). Supported by these experimental and histological findings, the MgH 2 -Gel met the criteria of the Chinese National Standard (GB/T 16886.23/ISO 10993-23) for the biological evaluation of medical devices with respect to skin irritation, as evidenced by a CMA (China Metrology Accreditation)-certified report (Supplementary Material_GB/T 16886.23 Report).

In the etiopathogenesis of psoriasis, the abnormal activation and hyperproliferation of keratinocytes (KC) have long been recognized as a pivotal step in symptom manifestation. To assess the influence on the vitality and proliferation of keratinocytes, MgH 2 nanoparticles of different amounts were then co-cultured with keratinocytes (HaCaTs) by employing a transwell setup (A). As was revealed in B and C, the vitality of keratinocytes gradually diminished in parallel with the increment of MgH 2 concentrations. The intervention dose at which keratinocyte viability was inhibited by 50% in vitro was then determined as of 519.6 μg/ml.

The optimal dose of MgH 2 nanoparticles for suppressing HaCaT proliferation was also tested at concentrations of 350 μg/ml, 500 μg/ml, and 700 μg/ml. Cell viability was assessed at 24 h, 48 h, and 72 h. With increased co-incubation periods (interfering time), a similar trend of markedly decreased viability was observed across all three concentrations (D and E). Specifically, the cellular capacity for DNA synthesis and proliferation was effectively inhibited at 500 μg/ml in HaCaTs (F–G and S14 ). The as-prepared MgH 2 nanoparticles was thus demonstrated with significant effectiveness in suppressing the vitalities and overproliferation of keratinocytes in vitro , presumably due to the long-term exposure to abundant hydrogen generated during reaction of MgH 2 in aqueous media, though may be coupled with the influence of other reaction byproducts.

Glycolysis and oxidative stress can synergistically interfere with keratinocyte proliferation. As reported, the hyperproliferation, abnormal differentiation, and metabolic hyperactivity of keratinocytes in psoriasis lesions are similar to that of tumor cells, relying on aerobic glycolysis, rather than tricarboxylic acid cycle to generate ATP, even when oxygen is available [,]. According to the evidence presented, the intervention in the KC glycolysis and its metabolic processes could be a potential therapeutic target for psoriasis. The specific inhibition of the glycolysis-related enzyme activity, such as the M2 isoform of the glycolytic enzyme pyruvate kinase (PKM2), may also impair KC proliferative capacity by promoting macrophage activation and increasing TNF- α secretion []. To explore the hypothesis of whether MgH 2 might exert an impact on the KC glycolysis, the expression of PKM2, an enzyme that serves as a pivotal rate-limiting factor in pro-inflammatory pathways, was measured via the Western blot assay. While a rise of PKM2 expression was found in the skin lesions of psoriasis, surprisingly, after exposed to MgH 2 (500 μg/ml) for 24 h, the expression of PKM2 drastically decreased to a great extent (H and I). To elucidate the targets of MgH 2 within this pathway, we utilized the STRING database to construct a protein-protein interaction (PPI) network for PKM2. This bioinformatic analysis identified HIF-1α (a key upstream regulator []) and LDHA (the enzyme responsible for the final conversion of pyruvate to lactate) as its closest interacting nodes (). Guided by these predictions, we subsequently evaluated their protein expression via Western blot. While MgH 2 significantly suppressed HIF-1α expression in HaCaT cells, LDHA protein levels remained largely unchanged (). Despite stable LDHA expression, downstream lactate production, along with intracellular ATP and glucose utilization, markedly declined (K and L). This suggests that the reduction in glycolytic end-products is primarily driven by upstream substrate depletion—specifically, by a blockade at the PKM2 step—rather than by direct downregulation of LDHA protein. Collectively, these data indicate that MgH 2 specifically disrupts the hyperactive HIF-1α/PKM2 in keratinocytes.

To further corroborate the downstream metabolic consequences of PKM2 inhibition, untargeted LC-MS was performed to analyze the metabolites before and after MgH 2 intervention. As illustrated in the KEGG pathway classification (A), the differentially expressed metabolites were primarily clustered in “Carbohydrate metabolism” and “Energy metabolism”. Furthermore, KEGG enrichment analysis (B) highlighted significant alterations in specific pathways tightly linked to glucose utilization, including “Carbon metabolism”, the “TCA cycle”, and “Oxidative phosphorylation”. These downstream metabolomic shifts are highly consistent with our observed suppression of PKM2 and ATP production. Collectively, the LC-MS data provide metabolic evidence reinforcing our conclusion that MgH 2 restricts the hyperactive glycolytic flux in psoriatic keratinocytes.

The pathological role of ROS and oxidative stress is attracting intensified attention during the formation and development of psoriasis, particularly in the step involving activation of transcription factors in keratinocytes []. To elucidate the antioxidative effects of MgH 2 , we detected the quantification of ROS expression levels within HaCaTs upon subjected to co-incubation with MgH 2 nanoparticles of two concentrations (350 μg/ml and 500 μg/ml). ROS, which was inevitably generated as active free radicals (e.g. ·OH, ONOO − ) during cellular metabolisms, are the primary substances causing oxidative damage to tissues upon excessive accumulation []. With the interference of MgH 2 , the ROS levels declined substantially in HaCaTs, thus showing promise in restoring the intracellular redox homeostasis. Notably, with the treatment of 500 μg/ml MgH 2 , a more striking decrease in the ROS expression was found when compared with that of the 350 μg/ml group (C and D).

It has been extensively acknowledged that elevated levels of ROS play a pivotal role in the onset, advancement, and resolution of inflammatory processes, accompanied by multifactorial inflammatory cytokines [,]. In an attempt to probe the potential inflammation modulatory effect, HaCaTs were pretreated with LPS. After a 30-min pretreatment, the cells were subsequently exposed to MgH 2 particles (500 μg/ml) and collected 24 h later. The RT-qPCR results of mRNA expressions of major pro-inflammatory cytokines, including TNF- α , IL-1 β, and CCL20, key molecules in the formation of psoriasis lesion, indicated that MgH 2 pretreatment would lower their transcriptions under LPS stimuli (E–G). These results proved the potent ROS-scavenging and anti-inflammation characteristics of MgH 2 particles for HaCaTs.

MgH 2 -Gel, which was fabricated as above described with self-generation of bulk microbubbles “locking” hydrogen gas for sustained local release, had been identified as a non-skin irritant prior to the in vivo efficiency experiment. To explore the therapeutic effects on psoriasis administration, MgH 2 -Gel was topically applied to the imiquimod (IMQ)-induced mice psoriasis model with different doses (1 mg/ml and 5 mg/ml), in comparison with the blank control group of IMQ (untreated) (A and B and S17 ). Apart from these, to further identify the contribution of local hydrogen supply from the MgH 2 -Gel for psoriasis treatment, blank Gel, MgCl 2 -Gel, and NaOH-Gel groups were also established as additional controls, and the release of reaction byproducts (namely, released Mg 2+ and elevated alkalinity) during MgH 2 -Gel application could be respectively distinguished in . The in vivo results clearly revealed that MgH 2 -Gel of both concentrations improved the psoriasis-like lesion significantly. It is noteworthy that, in a short-term treatment regimen, magnesium hydrogen gel demonstrated a more rapid alleviation of psoriasis lesions compared to the clinical calcipotriol treatment. This finding indicates that magnesium hydrogen gel may offer a significant advantage in the expedited relief of psoriasis.

Moreover, even under low-dose MgH 2 -Gel (1 mg/ml) intervention, the erythema (PASI: 3.16 vs 2.33) and scaling (PASI: 3.83 vs 1.16) of the psoriasis-like lesions were ameliorated, and meanwhile, the infiltration score of the lesions was reduced (PASI: 3.33 vs 1.33). Such desirable improvement in erythema (PASI: 3.16 vs 1.00), scaling (PASI: 3.83 vs 1.16), and lesion infiltration (PASI: 3.33 vs 1.00) of psoriasis-like lesions was more significant with high-dose MgH 2 -Gel (5 mg/ml) intervention. The epidermal thickness significantly improved after MgH 2 -Gel (1 mg/ml) and (5 mg/ml) treatment, respectively, as (0.735 vs 0.627 mm) and (0.735 vs 0.517 mm). For clear comparisons (C–F), a slight to mild amelioration of psoriasis-like lesions was achieved with the administration of calcipotriol therapy. No visible lesion changes were found in the blank Gel and NaOH-Gel groups, thus ruling out the possible impact of gel matrix and the alkaline pH. Intriguingly, the scale scores in the MgCl 2 -Gel group were found slightly improved, which was presumably correlated to the anti-inflammatory effects of Mg 2+ ions [].

Hematoxylin-eosin (HE) and CK-16 immunohistochemical staining were used to assess the pathologic changes in different treatment groups. The HE staining results revealed that the skin tissues in the IMQ-induced mice presented typical psoriasis changes, which included hyperkeratinization accompanied with parakeratosis, acanthosis, elongated trochanterellus, and infiltrated inflammatory cells. These pathological manifestations thus demonstrated the successful establishment of the psoriasis mice model. CK-16 was recognized as the marker signifying the extent of hyperkeratinization of keratinocytes, of which low expression was usually found in normal skin []. In the IMQ group, a marked increase of CK-16 was observed. The treatment with MgH 2 -Gel (5 mg/ml and 1 mg/ml) markedly led to a diminished hyperkeratinization, inflammatory infiltration, acanthosis, and CK-16 expression. The reduction extent was also positive correlated to the applied concentration of MgH 2 -Gel. Meanwhile, the Calcipotriol group, as well as the blank Gel, MgCl 2 -Gel, and NaOH-Gel groups, did not exhibit complete restoration despite the observed improvement (). All these findings manifested that MgH 2 -Gel could effectively ameliorate the symptoms of psoriasis lesions. Furthermore, by comparison, it was clearly confirmed in vivo that the major therapeutic effects could be attributable to the continuous, local H 2 release, rather than blank hydrogel, or elevated pH, while Mg 2+ might also play a slight, anti-inflammatory role in amelioration of skin lesions.

The bioeffects of MgH 2 -Gel were further demonstrated via immunohistochemical staining of the skin lesions with PCNA and Ki-67. PCNA and Ki-67 are the cellular proliferation markers. As expected, these expressions of mouse keratinocytes were both greatly elevated in the IMQ-induced psoriasis group [,]. After the MgH 2 -Gel treatment, we found a simultaneous reduction of both expressions in the keratinocytes (G). Notably, such changes in PCNA, and Ki-67 were not observed in the Calcipotriol, MgCl 2 -Gel, NaOH-Gel groups, or blank Gel (), confirming the anti-hyperplasia capacity of MgH 2 -Gel was only stemmed from sufficient hydrogen release.

Furthermore, MgH 2 -Gel was found to down-regulate the nucleotide metabolism in psoriasis. Nucleotide metabolism is vital to cellular proliferation and differentiation, as it plays a crucial role in various physiological processes, including the regulation of carbohydrate metabolism. The increased demand for nucleotides by proliferating cells for the synthesis of ribosomal RNA, replication of the genome, and maintenance of the transcriptome puts nucleotide synthesis in a special position in proliferating cell metabolism []. LS/MS metabolomics was thus used for the analysis of the metabolite changes in the pre-and post-interference lesions with MgH 2 -Gel (5 mg/ml) (A). As shown in B, the nucleotide metabolism-related metabolite levels in the IMQ-induced mice were elevated as compared with the normal controls, while a remarkable decrease of metabolite levels was revealing after MgH 2 -Gel treatment, among which the change of Uracil/Adenine/dCMP/dAMP/UDP-GlcNAc metabolic levels achieved statistical significance. Taken together, it was reasonably speculated that the inhibition of KC growth activity by MgH 2 -Gel was probably via the downregulation of nucleotide metabolism.

The metabolic characteristics and activity are a pivotal determinant for the rate of keratinocyte proliferation [].To investigate the effect of MgH 2 -Gel on glycolysis in psoriatic lesions, PKM2 protein expression was detected with Western Blot assay. The expression of PKM2 was increased in psoriatic mice compared with normal controls, but could be greatly decreased after MgH 2 -Gel treatment, which was consistent with the cellular results (C and D). Furthermore, we evaluated HIF-1α and LDHA expression. Mirroring the in vitro cellular findings, HIF-1α was significantly downregulated in the tissues of the MgH 2 -Gel group, whereas the expression of LDHA remained largely unchanged (E and F, ). These in vivo results align perfectly with our cellular experiments, further confirming that MgH 2 -Gel modulates the glycolytic pathway.

To further elucidate the bioeffect of MgH2 on glucose metabolism, the group treated with MgH2-Gel (5 mg/mL) was used to investigate alterations in pertinent metabolites pre- and post-intervention. Metabolites associated with glucose metabolism in IMQ mice increased compared with normal control, and returned to homeostatic levels after MgH 2 -Gel treatment.Metabolomic analysis revealed that succinic acid, a key tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle intermediate [], was significantly decreased in IMQ-induced lesions but markedly upregulated following MgH 2 -Gel treatment (G). α-ketoglutarate (AKG), another TCA cycle intermediate metabolite, showed a comparable restoration pattern. Conversely, lactic acid, the terminal glycolysis product, was upregulated after IMQ intervention and significantly downregulated by MgH 2 -Gel treatment []. Differential abundance (DA) score analysis of KEGG pathways based on LC-MS/MS metabolomics data demonstrated significant enrichment of differential metabolites in the glycolysis pathway within psoriasis-like lesions compared to the MgH 2 -Gel treatment group. In contrast, enrichment in other glucose metabolism pathways, including starch and sucrose metabolism and galactose metabolism, was reduced considerably (H). Notably, the galactose metabolism pathway can serve as an alternative to glycolysis with lower lactate yield []. Combined with the observed downregulation of the rate-limiting glycolytic enzyme PKM2, these findings indicate the presence of an aerobic Warburg effect—characterized by preferential glucose metabolism via glycolysis for proliferation despite oxygen availability—in IMQ-induced lesions. MgH 2 intervention effectively reprogrammed this metabolic phenotype.

The total oxidative stress levels in psoriasis are significantly elevated, accompanied by a decrease of CAT and SOD []. We found the expression of SOD (716.3 vs 538.4 U/mg) and CAT (26.55 vs 12.27 U/mg) in the skin lesions of IMQ mice was significantly reduced, but could return to the level of control after MgH 2 -Gel treatment (J), indicating that MgH 2 -Gel with continuous, controlled hydrogen delivery can effectively bring down oxidative stress levels in psoriatic lesions, in turn re-establishing endogenous redox homeostasis in vivo . To further corroborate these findings, we evaluated the levels of 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE), a well-established biomarker for tissue oxidative damage [], in the skin lesions across the IMQ, MgCl 2 -Gel, and MgH 2 -Gel groups. As shown in , MgH 2 -Gel intervention significantly reduced 4-HNE accumulation in tissues. In contrast, the MgCl 2 -Gel treatment failed to exhibit a similar reduction, thereby underscoring the comprehensive superiority of the MgH 2 gel as a magnesium-based hydrogen-donating therapeutic system.

In response to oxidative stress, KC-derived cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6) to stimulate DCs to secrete IL-23, which promotes TH17 cell differentiation and activation. As both initiators and amplifiers, KCs are activated and driven to hyperproliferate by inflammatory cytokines secreted from TH17 cells (IL-17 and IL-22) and inflammatory dendritic cells (DCs)(IL-23, nitric oxide (NO), and TNF), which thereby initiates and fuels a inflammation vicious cycle (I [,]. We applied high-throughput sequencing via a Quantibody mouse cytokine array to assess inflammation cytokines before and after the MgH 2 -Gel intervention (K and L). The general expression of inflammatory cytokines experienced a sharp decline after the MgH 2 -Gel intervention, verifying a potent anti-inflammatory effect in vivo . Notably, key cytokines central to the KC-driven inflammatory vicious cycle – including IL-6, IL-22, and IL-23 exhibited statistically significant reductions in expression following MgH 2 -Gel treatment []. This comprehensive dampening of pro-inflammatory mediators underscores the potent anti-inflammatory efficacy of the localized hydrogen therapy.

Following the schematic protocol provided in A and B, we identified the role of MgH 2 -Gel in mitigating psoriasis relapse in a murine model of relapse. During the IMQ-induced phase, immunofluorescence staining revealed a remarkable reduction in the expression of CD69 and CD103—surface markers associated with the residency of tissue-resident memory T (TRM) cells, which play a key role in driving recurrence in situ (C–F). MgH 2 -Gel treatment significantly attenuated the recurrence of psoriasis-like lesions, as evidenced by statistically improved PASI scores (G–I) and a reduction in epidermal thickness (J). Topical MgH 2 -Gel administration notably attenuated key histopathological hallmarks of psoriasis in H&E-stained sections, including concomitant reductions in parakeratosis, acanthosis, and Munro microabscesses (K).

To elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying the sustained therapeutic effect and potential prevention of relapse, we conducted RNA sequencing on skin lesions from the Relapse and Relapse + MgH 2 groups. Gene Ontology(GO)enrichment analysis of differentially expressed genes revealed robust enrichment in biological processes specifically related to mitochondrial proton-transporting ATP synthase activity and NADH dehydrogenase activity (L). Consistently, reactome enrichment analysis further demonstrated significant and coordinated regulation of pathways governing the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle , mitochondrial respiratory electron transport, and keratinization (M). Collectively, MgH 2 -Gel simultaneously targets TRM residency and metabolic regulation in psoriasis relapse.
sections.discussion:
Psoriasis is a chronic, immune-mediated disease driven by a dysregulated keratinocyte (KC) immune-inflammatory axis. Disrupting this pathogenetic vicious cycle is critical for achieving sustained remission []. Oxidative stress, inflammatory cytokines, and energy metabolism play a significant pathogenic role in the occurrence of psoriasis [,,,]. Despite advances in biologic agents and small molecular medicine therapies, disease relapse still frequently occurs at prior lesion sites. TRM residency is strongly related with psoriatic recurrence in situ as indicated by surface markers CD69 and CD103 expression [,]. Consequently, an unmet need remains for topical agents that concurrently target these tripartite pathogenic mechanisms while demonstrating high efficacy, safety, and tolerability to achieve lesion clearance and prevent recurrence.

In a recent clinical report, Ping et al. first demonstrated that the hydrogen generated during water electrolysis, combined with bathing therapy, effectively ameliorated the itching symptoms and lesions of psoriasis patients []. Nevertheless, the high expenses, complicated preparation procedures, and inconvenience to medication compliance largely hampered the further application of such hydrogen-water bathing treatment. Realizing sufficient and long-term H 2 delivery is vital to therapeutic efficacy and essential for clinical translation. However, traditional administration routes are hampered by the high diffusibility and low solubility of gaseous H 2 . Despite the very recent progress in developing hydrogen-delivery biomaterials, their feasibility often suffers from inadequate local hydrogen supply or bearing biosafety concerns, thus imposing an unresolved obstacle at present. In this work, we came up with an innovative hydrogen microbubble gel imparting abundant and prolonged local delivery of H 2 for psoriasis treatment, along with the underlying therapeutic mechanisms clarified. Upon continuous generation of H 2 by spontaneous hydrolysis of MgH 2 in the saline-containing hydrogel, this light-weight, easy-escaping gas could be immediately “stored” and “locked” via amounts of stabilized microbubble formation within the gel matrix, thus restraining the burst release of H 2 . It should be noted that the pathological environment of psoriasis is characterized by a slightly acidic condition. While our in vitro results in physiological saline provide a baseline for H 2 release, the localized acidic environment might slightly accelerate the initial hydrolysis of MgH 2 . Moreover, the high diffusivity of H 2 ensures that it can bypass the thickened skin barrier to exert anti-inflammatory effects in the deeper dermis. However, in vivo direct quantification of hydrogen distribution across skin was difficult in the present study. This is primarily due to the intrinsic properties of hydrogen, including its extremely high diffusivity and optical invisibility, which preclude real-time detection in living skin using currently available technologies. As a result, assessment of hydrogen retention in gas-based therapies commonly relies on indirect evidence, such as sustained release kinetics and durable biological responses. The prolonged therapeutic efficacy observed in vivo in our study supports the biological relevance of localized hydrogen availability, while acknowledging that hydrogen spatial distribution awaits future technical advances. Moreover, hydrogel delivery represents a mature and highly biocompatible technology; it is non-invasive, causes no trauma to the skin, and ensures an excellent safety profile for topical application [,].

Mechanistically, this localized hydrogen treatment exerts its profound bioeffects not through a single pathway but through coordinated modulation of the oxidative, inflammatory, and metabolic microenvironments. First, we identified that MgH 2 -Gel effectively disrupts the hyperactive metabolic state of psoriatic keratinocytes. Guided by STRING database predictions, we observed that MgH 2 intervention significantly downregulated the HIF-1α and PKM2. Interestingly, although the downstream enzyme LDHA expression remained unchanged, intracellular lactate and ATP production markedly declined, indicating that the reduction in glycolytic end-products is primarily driven by upstream substrate depletion following PKM2 blockade. Furthermore, our LC-MS and KEGG enrichment analyses confirmed that this intervention triggers a broader systemic metabolic shift that affects central carbon metabolism and the TCA cycle, thereby counteracting the Warburg-like metabolic reprogramming characteristic of psoriasis.

Concurrently, MgH 2 -Gel robustly suppressed epidermal hyperproliferation (indicated by decreased PCNA and Ki67) and re-established endogenous redox homeostasis (evidenced by reduced 4-HNE). While the baseline anti-inflammatory properties of magnesium ions (Mg 2+ ) are well evidenced [,], parallel evaluation of the MgCl 2 -Gel control group revealed that Mg 2+ alone failed to achieve significant reductions in PCNA, Ki67, or 4-HNE, nor did it drive extensive metabolic corrections. This distinct contrast suggests that the profound therapeutic efficacy observed is fundamentally driven by the synergistic integration of sustained H 2 release within the magnesium-based platform. Beyond acute lesion clearance, the MgH 2 -Gel also exhibited significant potential in relapse intervention. It alleviates recurrence and downregulates T-cell residency, which plays a key role in recurrence.

Despite these highly encouraging outcomes, we acknowledge certain limitations in the present study. First, while our multi-omics and in vitro data demonstrate a strong association between H 2 intervention, glycolytic downregulation, and phenotypic improvement, these findings mainly demonstrate correlation rather than strict causality. Therefore, the underlying molecular causality regarding the specific mechanisms of MgH 2 -Gel intervention in the occurrence and recurrence of psoriasis-like lesions (e.g., via genetic perturbation) remains to be further investigated. Second, our exploratory comparison against calcipotriol monotherapy demonstrated pronounced short-term amelioration of lesion severity; however, longer-term comparative studies with regimens aligned to clinical maintenance dosing are necessary to comprehensively evaluate overall long-term superiority. Importantly, standard chronic dermal irritation tests (GB/T 16886.23/ISO 10993-23) and organ histological analyses have confirmed the biosafety of the formulation, supporting its translational potential.

Taken together, we herein present a local, sustained H 2 -generation and -delivery system with great biosafety that substantially ameliorate psoriasis-like symptoms and reduce psoriasis relapse in mice models. In conjunction of advantages of facile, cost-effective fabrication and ease of application, this in-situ hydrogenated microbubble gel treatment strategy holds great promise as a superior candidate for topical management of psoriasis, while comprehensive investigations of large-scale clinical trials for long-term use are required prior to its translation into clinical practice. Our proof-of-concept study not only reinforces the therapeutic potential of MgH 2 -based biomaterials but also paves the way for diverse applications of hydrogen medicine in treating a variety of inflammatory skin diseases and oxidative stress-related disorders.
sections.methods:
MgH 2 powders of uniform sub-microscale dispersion (termed as HydroMg) were prepared using an Arc Plasma Evaporation apparatus. A procedure involving arc evaporation of pure Mg along with in-situ hydrogenation was employed as we reported previously []. In detail, commercially available pure Mg powders with 99.9 % in purity were first compressed at room temperature to construct cylinders by a uniaxial compressor under a pressure of 25 MPa. Then, these cylinders, as anode materials, were put into a reaction chamber filled with mixed Ar (0.75 atm) and H 2 gas (0.05 atm) after the chamber was evacuated to below 5 × 10 −2 Pa. The direct current is set at 140 A during arc evaporation. Finally, before being taken out from the reaction chamber, the as-prepared HydroMg particles were subjected to passivation in air.

The morphologies of MgH 2 were investigated by TEM (120 KV, Talos L120C G2, USA). The size distribution of MgH 2 was analyzed by the Nano ZS90 Series particle size analyzer. XRD data was measured by using a D8 DaVinci diffractometer (Bruker, Germany) operated at 40 kV.

15g, 20g, and 25 g of F127 (15 wt%, 20 wt%, 25 wt%) was added in physiological saline solution (0.9% NaCl, 100 mL) at 4 °C to fully dissolve to obtain temperature-sensitive hydrogel precursor solutions. The tube tilting method was performed to determine the GFT of gels. The sample solution (1 mL) was added to the sample tube and observed while slowly heating the tube in the water bath at the range of 20 °C-37 °C. At each temperature, samples were equilibrated for a moment and visually observed by tilting the tube. The MgH 2 -Gel was prepared through a facile mixing and self-assembly method. Briefly, a blank gel was prepared by adding different amounts of F127 (Sigma-Aldrich, USA) into a physiological saline solution (0.9% NaCl). The mixture was stirred with a magnetic stirrer in a 4 °C refrigerator until a clear sol solution was formed. Then, it underwent gelling by mixing the MgH 2 particles, or MgSO 4 solution, or NaOH solution, and the blank gel solution was stored at 4 °C before use according to the designated concentration.

The measurement was conducted in a wide-mouth cylindrical bottle where the hydrogel (1 mL, Concentration of MgH 2 :1 mg/ml) was cast to completely cover the bottom, then adding 2 mL 0.9% NaCl solution. A calibrated hydrogen microsensor multimeter (MMS-903995, UNISENSE, Denmark) was vertically inserted through the bottle opening and positioned above gel (1 cm) precisely using a micromanipulator (). To examine the gas composition entrapped in the hydrogel, we conducted Gas Chromatography (GC) analysis using gas chromatograph (Nexi GC 2030, SHIMADZU, Japan) equipped with a Barrier Discharge Ionization Detector (BID). The values of H 2 concentration dissolved in saline, pH, and the concentration of Mg 2+ were recorded at different time points using a hydrogen measurement meter (ENH-2000, TRUSTLEX, Japan), compact pH meter (LAQUAtwin-pH-22, HORIBA Advanced Techno, Japan) and Inductively Coupled Plasma analysis (iCAP6300, Thermo Fisher, USA), respectively.

Human immortalized keratinocytes (HaCaT) cell lines were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (Manassas, MD, USA) and were cultured in Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium (Gibco, Waltham, USA) supplemented with 10% FBS (Gibco, USA), penicillin (100 U/mL) and streptomycin (100 U/ml) (Gibco, USA). The cells were incubated in an atmosphere containing 5% CO2 and 37 °C humidified at 37 °C. The CCK8 kit (Dojindo, Japan) was used to evaluate cell viability following the manufacturer's instructions. After inoculating HaCaT cells into 96-well plates and cultured until reaching 40-50% confluence, the cells were treated with MgH 2 particles for periods of 8, 12, 24, 48, and 72 h, respectively. Each well was placed with 10 μL of CCK-8 solutions, followed by 90 μL of fresh medium, and the plates were incubated for 1 h at 37 °C. An enzyme marker (Multiskan GO, Thermo Fisher, USA) with a wavelength of 450 nm was used in the experiment.

Ribobio of China provided the EdU (5-ethynyl-2′-deoxyuridine) 488, Imaging Kit. The cells were treated with 50 M EdU at 37 °C for a duration of 2 h. Cells were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (Sigma-Aldrich, USA) for 15 min before being permeabilized with 0.5% Triton X100 for 10 min. The Apollo 488 solution and Hoechst 33342 were then used to stain the cells. The ratio of EdU-positive cells (green cells) to total Hoechst-positive cells (blue cells) represents the cells' ability to synthesize DNA.

The ATP content was assessed using the Enhanced ATP Assay Kit (Beyotime, China). After compression treatment, NPSCs were lysed with the ATP lysis buffer. Subsequently, the supernatant was harvested through centrifugation and subjected to a reaction with the ATP detection working dilution. (12,000 g, 5 min). The luminescence activity was detected by luminescence spectrometry (EnSpire, United States). The ATP level was normalized to cellular protein concentration.

The generation of ROS was measured by flow cytometry and 2′, 7′-dichlorodihydrofluorescein diacetate (DCFH-DA) (Sigma-Aldrich). For 24 h, media with varying doses of MgH 2 (350 μg/ml; 500 μg/ml) was treated with HaCaT (10 5 cells/well). Prior to the treatment with DCFH-DA, cells were collected, centrifuged (at 1000 rpm for 5 min), and washed with 1 mL of PBS (20 M). After 20 min of incubation, the fluorescence was detected by flow cytometry (BD LSRFortessa, USA): excitation/emission wavelengths: 488 nm/525 nm.

The separated epidermis or the pretreatment cells were subjected to total protein extraction using RIPA Lysis Buffer (Beyotime, China), which was enhanced with phenylmethanesulfonyl fluoride (1 mM) (Beyotime). BCA protein assay reagents were used to measure the protein concentration (Beyotime). The protein samples obtained were subjected to electrophoretic separation using a precast gel provided by Tanon (China). Following this, they were transferred onto a polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membrane after the assessment of their concentration. β-actin and PKM2 primary antibodies (1:1000 each) and secondary antibodies (1:1000, Beyotime) were incubated on the membranes at 4 °C overnight, and for 50 min, respectively. The membrane was detected using an improved chemiluminescence technique following three washes with Tris-buffered saline with Tween (TBST) solution.

The PCR primers were produced by BioTNT (Shanghai, China). Amplification reactions were carried out using SYBR Premix EX Taq II (Takara) on the 7500 real-time PCR system (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA, USA). The β -actin housekeeping gene was used to normalize gene expression, while the data were represented as fold differences by the 2 −ΔΔCt method, with ΔCt = Ct target gene − Ct β -actin , and ΔΔCt = ΔCt induced − ΔCt reference .

The primer sequences are as follows:

β-actin: forward primer 5′ TAAGGTGACAGCAGTCGGTT 3′, reverse primer 5′ TGTGTGGACTTGGGAGAGG 3’;

TNF-alpha: forward primer 5′ CAG GAC TTG AGA AGA CCT CAC 3′, reverse primer 5′ GTC TGG AAA CAT CTG GAG AGA 3';

CCL20: forward primer 5′ GAC ATA GCC CAA GAA CAG AAA 3′, reverse primer 5′ CCA GTG AGG CAC AAA TTA GAT 3';

IL1Beta: forward primer 5′ GAT ATG GAG CAA CAA GTG GT 3′, reverse primer 5′ AGG ACA GGT ACA GAT TCT TTT C 3';

CD69: forward primer 5′ GTA CGA GAA GTT GGA ATC ATC TG 3’, reverse primer 5′ GTT GTG GTG GAG AAG AAG TAA CAT 3';

CD103: forward primer 5′ TCT CCA GAT GTT CAG TGT GAT G 3’, reverse primer 5′ CTT GAG TAT GGG GTG ACC AAT 3'.

Male BALB/c mice (7-weeks old) were acquired from Shanghai Jihui Laboratory Animal Care Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China) and maintained under specific pathogen-free conditions in a controlled environment provided by the Department of Laboratory Animal Science, Fudan University (Shanghai, China). All animal experiments were meticulously executed in stringent adherence to the protocols outlined in the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals, as mandated by Fudan University. The protocol was approved by the Animal Welfare and Ethics Group, Department of Laboratory Animal Science, Fudan University (Permit No. 2020-Huashan hospital-JS-294). The ethical principles of experimental animal welfare were followed throughout the entirety of the experimental protocols, and every effort was made to minimize animal suffering.

Each mouse was shaved on the back after 1 week of acclimatization feeding with an area of 2∗3 cm to induce skin inflammation. Every 24 h for 7 days, IMQ cream (5%) was applied to the shaved area on the back of the experimented mouse (50 mg/mouse), and the induced skin lesion was photographed and observed on day 8 to obtain the PASI score, and the dorsal skin thickness was measured using a digital micrometer (Mitutoyo) as well (randomly take measurements at three different locations on the skin and calculate the average). To be specific, all the mice in this study were divided into eight groups: group 1 (normal mice), group 2 (mice treated with IMQ only and induced psoriasis), group 3 (mice with psoriasis treated with 1 mg/ml MgH 2 -Gel), group 4 (mice with psoriasis treated with 5 mg/ml MgH 2 -Gel), group 5 (mice wihth psoriasis with calcipotriol), group 6 (mice with psoriasis with Gel intervention), group 7 (mice with psoriasis and with MgCL 2 -Gel/intervention as a control) and group 8 (mice with psoriasis and NaOH-Gel intervention as a control). Groups 2, 6, 7, and 8 were designated as the negative control groups.

The murine model of psoriasis relapse was established as described by Shi et al. []. Imiquimod (IMQ; MedShine, Sichuan, China) at a dose of 62.5 mg was applied topically to the shaved area on the back of the mice for 7 consecutive days. Following a 30-day rest interval, IMQ (20.8 mg) was reapplied for 7 consecutive days to induce psoriasis relapse.

An objective scoring system was developed to assess the extent and severity of inflammation in the dorsal lesions in mice with psoriasis according to the PASI clinical criteria. Erythema and scale were graded on a scale of 0 to 4 (0, none; 1, mild; 2, moderate; 3, severe; 4, extremely severe).

The dorsal skin lesion samples in each group were collected on day 8 (occurrence)/day 48 (recurrence) and immobilized using a paraformaldehyde solution (4%). Subsequently, the paraffin-embedded fixed samples were dehydrated, dewaxed, rehydrated, and stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E). Besides, histopathological sections were examined with CK-16 (GB12804), PCNA (GB13010-1), and Ki67 ( GB111141 ) antibodies. After reaction with these primary antibodies, the section samples were probed with appropriate secondary antibodies conjugated with horseradish peroxidase (HRP), followed by color development with diaminobenzidine (Dako, CA, USA), and restained with hematoxylin (Si).

Tissue samples were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde and incubated with primary antibodies including rabbit anti-CD69 (Absinbio, abs136297), rabbit anti-CD103(Absinbio, abs118732). Following overnight incubation at 4 °C, samples were stained with secondary antibodies (Alexa Fluor 555 anti-rabbit IgG and Alexa Fluor 488 anti-mouse IgG, both 1:2000, Cell Signaling Technology) at room temperature. DAPI (Dako, Glostrup, Denmark) served as a nuclear counterstain. Slides were examined using a confocal laser scanning microscope (FV-1000, Olympus, Tokyo, Japan).

The meticulously thawed sample was accurately weighed to 50 mg and transferred into a 2 mL EP tube, with the addition of 500 μL of pre-cooled extractant (70% methanol aqueous solution). A small steel ball was also added to the EP tube. Following this procedure, the EP tube was homogenized 4 times at 30 Hz, for 30 s each time. After homogenization, the tube was shaken at 1500 r/min for 5 min, then stood for 15 min on ice, and subsequently centrifuged with 12000 r/min at 4 °C for 10 min. Finally, 200 μL of supernatant was put into the vial designated for subsequent LC-MS/MS analysis.

Total RNA was extracted from full-thickness mouse skin samples using TRIzol reagent. RNA was extracted from PBMCs and prepared for transcriptomic analysis. mRNA was purified using oligo(dT)-coated magnetic beads and libraries were constructed for sequencing on the Illumina HiSeq 2000 platform, generating 50-nt single-end reads. Library quality was assessed using the Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer, and raw reads were processed with Trimmomatic software for further analysis.

SOD and CAT assay kits (Beyotime Biotechnology) were used for the evaluation of SOD and CAT activity, respectively. The glucose production was quantitatively analyzed utilizing the Glucose Assay Kit (Njjcbio, China), following the detailed protocol provided by the manufacturer.

Skin lesions from psoriatic mice, normal mice, and mice in the MgH 2 -Gel group were processed and proteins were extracted according to the manual of Protein Array (Ray Biotech, Inc, USA). The custom Quantibody mouse cytokine array was used. This assay utilizes a multiplex sandwich enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) system featuring a membrane embedded with antibodies targeting specific cytokines or chemokines. The procedure followed the detailed protocol provided in the operation manual. Each cytokine-specific antibody was methodically arrayed in quadruplicate, with positive controls, negative controls, and internal controls similarly arranged. Data were extracted and analyzed using the RayBio QAM-TH17-1 software (RayBiotech, Inc.). For the cytokine levels below the assay sensitivity threshold, a value of 0 was used instead when comparing the levels.

Four Balb/c mice were used to assess the skin irritation potential of MgH 2 . The dorsal region was depilated using hair clippers 24 h prior to the initiation of the irritation experiment. MgH 2 was applied uniformly to the hairless skin regions (area A and D for 5 days, while the hairless skin regions (area B and C) were left untreated for the sake of comparisons (). After the application of MgH 2 , the hairless skin was observed for any possible reactions, mostly redness, and erythema. During this skin irritation test, we referred to the scoring criteria (irritation index) in ISO-10993-10, in which a score of erythema and edema (ranging from 0 to 4) was recorded to reflect the extent of irritation. As illustrated, an irritation index lower than 0.4 indicated negligible irritation.

To further evaluate the systemic biosafety, histological analysis of major organs was also conducted. The mice were assigned into three groups: the control group, the Gel group (treated with blank gel), and the MgH 2 -Gel group. Major organs including the heart, liver, spleen, lung, and kidney were harvested, sectioned, and subjected to standard histological examination (H&E staining) to observe any potential systemic toxicity or pathological tissue damage.

The KEGG database is a useful tool for comprehending the important roles and uses of the biological system. We tested the statistical enrichment of differentially expressed genes in KEGG pathways utilizing the KOBAS software platform. The KEGG pathways that were highly enriched in comparison to the background of the entire genome were discovered using the Cluster Profiler R tools. Pathways that were highly enriched in differentially expressed genes were those having a Q value of 0.05.

Data are presented as the mean ± standard deviation (SD). Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS software (version 18.0; IBM, USA). Comparisons between two groups were analyzed using the unpaired two-tailed Student's t-test. For comparisons among multiple groups, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was applied. Importantly, to correct for multiple comparisons, Tukey's test was applied post hoc to assess the statistical significance of specific group pairs. A P-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

title: New-Onset Psoriatic Arthritis under Biologics in Psoriasis Patients: An Increasing Challenge?
abstract: Psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis (PsA) development is sustained by tumor necrosis factor (TNF)α, interleukin (IL)17, and IL23; hence, biologics targeting those cytokines represent useful therapeutic weapons for both conditions. Nevertheless, biologics strongly reduce PsA risk; several studies reported the possibility of new-onset PsA during biologic therapy for psoriasis. The aim of this 1-year prospective study is to evaluate the prevalence of paradoxical PsA in psoriasis patients under biologic therapy and review the existing literature. For each patient, age, sex, psoriasis duration, psoriasis severity, comorbidities, and previous and current psoriasis treatments were collected, and each subject was screened for PsA using the Early ARthritis for Psoriatic patient (EARP) questionnaire every 3 months for 1 year. New-onset PsA was diagnosed in 10 (8.5%) out of 118 patients (three male, 30.0%; mean age 44.5 years) involving every different biologic class (anti-TNF, anti-IL12/23, anti-IL17, and anti-IL23). No significant risk factor for new-onset PsA was identified; no significant difference was found comparing patients who developed PsA and subjects who did not develop PsA regarding psoriasis severity, past/current therapies, and comorbidities. Clinicians must keep in mind the possibility of PsA onset also in patients undergoing biologics so that PsA screening should be strongly recommended at each follow-up.
